verdict.summary:
ANSWER

The 1876 first edition of Robert's Rules of Order (the Pocket Manual, transcribed as Project Gutenberg ebook #9097) requires a TWO-THIRDS VOTE to adopt (order) a motion for the Previous Question. It is not a majority vote.

1. WHAT THE 1876 RULE SAYS (paraphrase, not a quotation)

In the 1876 manual the Previous Question is one of the subsidiary motions listed in order of precedence in Part I (Rules of Order), and the manual's article on the Previous Question states the vote required to adopt it: the motion is adopted only on a two-thirds vote. The manual also treats the motion as undebatable and not open to amendment, and it is put in the form 'Shall the main question be now put?' If the two-thirds vote is not obtained, the motion fails and debate on the pending question continues.

I am deliberately giving this as a close paraphrase rather than a verbatim quotation. The passages returned to me by the retrieval step did not include the operative sentence of the 1876 text (see 'Evidence status' below), and inventing quotation marks around a reconstructed sentence would misrepresent the source. The substantive point — two-thirds — is not in doubt.

2. EVIDENCE STATUS AND CONFIDENCE

- Direct grounding obtained: none on the operative sentence. The retrieved pages were (a) the Wikisource table of contents for the 1915 revised edition, which lists '29. The Previous Question ... 104' but does not state the vote requirement in the excerpt captured, and (b) an unrelated Hawaii County record page. Neither contradicts the answer; neither proves it.
- Basis for the answer: the standard text of the 1876 Pocket Manual, plus cross-edition continuity. The two-thirds requirement for the Previous Question appears in the 1876 first edition and is carried forward unchanged through the revised editions (1893, 1904, 1915), where the corresponding section on the Previous Question likewise requires a two-thirds vote. A rule that is stable across five editions is a low-risk answer for the first edition specifically.
- Confidence: high on the value (two-thirds); moderate on the exact sentence wording and on the 1876 article numbering (the 1876 manual's numbering is not the 1915 '§29' numbering, so a citation to '§29' would be an anachronism if applied to 1876).

3. HOW TO VERIFY IN THE GUTENBERG TEXT (procedure for whoever holds the file)

Step 1. Open the Project Gutenberg transcription of the 1876 edition (ebook #9097; the HTML file 9097-h.htm is the readable one). Confirm the front matter identifies the 1876 first edition / Pocket Manual rather than a revised edition — check the title page and copyright line, which in the revised editions carry later copyright dates.
Step 2. Search the text for the string 'Previous Question'. Expect several hits: the article devoted to the motion, plus the table of the order of precedence of motions.
Step 3. Read the article on the Previous Question. The sentence to locate is the one stating the vote required for adoption; it states two-thirds. Confirm you are reading the vote to ADOPT the motion, not the vote on the main question.
Step 4. If the transcription is a revised edition (1893 or later), the answer is still two-thirds — the requirement did not change — but the section number will be different and the surrounding procedural details will differ (see caveat below).
Step 5. Record the exact sentence verbatim from that page if a quotation is needed for the deliverable; do not reuse the paraphrase above as a quotation.

4. WHAT THE ANSWER DOES NOT COVER (scope discipline)

- The two-thirds applies to adopting/ordering the Previous Question. It does not change the vote required on the main question itself, which remains whatever that question otherwise requires (ordinarily a majority).
- The two-thirds is a fraction of the votes cast by members voting, which is how the manual's general rule treats a two-thirds vote — flagged as a general-rule point rather than a verified 1876 quotation.
- One genuine first-edition/modern difference, offered as context and not as part of the answer: in the 1876 edition, ordering the Previous Question closed debate on the main question together with the amendments pending to it, whereas later revisions narrowed the motion so that it applies only to the immediately pending question unless the mover specifies otherwise. This affects the EFFECT of the motion, not the two-thirds requirement, and is reported with moderate rather than high confidence.

5. BOTTOM LINE

Vote required to adopt a motion for the Previous Question under the 1876 first edition: two-thirds (2/3) of the votes cast — not a majority, and not unanimous consent.

verdict.summary:
# Luminous efficacy K_cd in the SI Brochure, 9th edition

## Direct answers

| Ask | Quantity | Fixed value | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation, *K*_cd | **683** (exact, by definition) | lm W⁻¹ (= cd sr W⁻¹ = cd sr kg⁻¹ m⁻² s³) |
| 2 | Frequency of that monochromatic radiation, ν | **540 × 10¹²** (= 540 THz = 5.4 × 10¹⁴ Hz) | Hz |

Both figures are fixed numerical values in the post-2019 SI: they are exact by definition and carry **no** experimental uncertainty.

## Normative wording (SI Brochure, 9th edition, 2019)

### 1. In the list of the seven defining constants (Chapter 2, section 2.3.1)

> "The International System of Units, the SI, is the system of units in which
> • the unperturbed ground state hyperfine transition frequency of the caesium 133 atom ∆ν_Cs is 9 192 631 770 Hz,
> • the speed of light in vacuum c is 299 792 458 m/s,
> • the Planck constant h is 6.626 070 15 × 10⁻³⁴ J s,
> • the elementary charge e is 1.602 176 634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C,
> • the Boltzmann constant k is 1.380 649 × 10⁻²³ J/K,
> • the Avogadro constant N_A is 6.022 140 76 × 10²³ mol⁻¹,
> • **the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10¹² hertz K_cd is 683 lm/W.**"

### 2. In Table 1, "The seven base units of the SI" (candela row)

> "The candela, symbol cd, is the SI unit of luminous intensity in a given direction. It is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10¹² Hz, K_cd, to be 683 when expressed in the unit lm W⁻¹, which is equal to cd sr W⁻¹, or cd sr kg⁻¹ m⁻² s³, where the kilogram, metre and second are defined in terms of h, c and ∆ν_Cs."

### 3. The exact relation the definition implies

> "This definition implies the exact relation K_cd = 683 cd sr kg⁻¹ m⁻² s³ for monochromatic radiation of frequency ν = 540 × 10¹² Hz."

### 4. The stated effect of the definition (the candela restated in words)

> "The effect of this definition is that one candela is the luminous intensity, in a given direction, of a source that emits monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10¹² Hz and has a radiant intensity in that direction of (1/683) W/sr."

### 5. Inverted relation, for completeness (candela expressed through defining constants)

> 1 cd = (1/683) K_cd (∆ν_Cs)² h · 6.626 070 15 × 10⁻³⁴ × (9 192 631 770)² ≈ 2.614 830 × 10¹⁰ (∆ν_Cs)² h K_cd

This inversion is the Brochure's own algebra; it is reproduced here only as context and does not alter either fixed value above.

## Points that must not be misread

1. **The defining quantity is a frequency, not a wavelength.** 540 × 10¹² Hz is the fixed specification. Any wavelength is a *derived* value obtained from λ = c/ν = 299 792 458 / (540 × 10¹²) m = 5.551 712 185… × 10⁻⁷ m ≈ 555 nm in vacuum (≈ 555.0 nm in standard air). The familiar "555 nm" figure is a convenience label for the green region near the maximum of the photopic luminous efficiency function V(λ); it is **not** part of the definition and must never be substituted for 540 THz when quoting the definition.
2. **No uncertainty is attached.** 683 lm/W is a *fixed numerical value*; the Brochure explicitly states that the definitions specify the exact numerical value of each constant. Do not write "683 ± …".
3. **Unit identity.** 683 lm/W = 683 cd sr W⁻¹ = 683 cd sr kg⁻¹ m⁻² s³. These are the same value expressed in three equivalent unit forms used in the Brochure; the numerical value 683 is unchanged.
4. **Provenance and version.** The values derive from the 26th CGPM (2018), which revised the SI to be based on fixed numerical values of seven defining constants; the 9th edition of the *SI Brochure* (BIPM, 2019) is the text that carries the revised definitions. The same 683 / 540 × 10¹² Hz pairing appears already in the draft of the ninth Brochure dated 5 February 2018, in the published 9th edition Table 1, and in the BIPM concise summary of the 9th edition — three mutually consistent BIPM sources, so no revision-dependent discrepancy exists for these two values. (Later corrigenda to the 9th edition correct typographical and cross-reference errors; they do not change defining constants, which are fixed by CGPM resolution and are not editable by the Brochure.)
5. **Prior SI status (for contrast only).** Before the 2019 revision the candela was defined via a 540 × 10¹² Hz monochromatic source of radiant intensity 1/683 W/sr; the 2019 wording converts this to a fixed value of *K*_cd. The number and the frequency are unchanged by that rewording — which is why both the pre- and post-2019 formulations yield the same two answers requested here.

## Verification checklist

- [x] Value of *K*_cd stated as 683 — matches all three fetched BIPM passages.
- [x] Unit stated as lm W⁻¹ — matches the defining-constants list; equivalent forms cd sr W⁻¹ and cd sr kg⁻¹ m⁻² s³ match Table 1 and section 2.3.1.
- [x] Frequency stated as 540 × 10¹² Hz — matches all three fetched BIPM passages, and is stated as a frequency in every one of them.
- [x] No uncertainty attached to either number (both exact by definition).

quotes.whole:
Editorial Note on Part 173
Editorial Note:
Nomenclature changes to part 173 appear at 70 FR 56098, Sept. 23, 2005.
§ 173.120 Class 3—Definitions.
(a) Flammable liquid.  For the purpose of this subchapter, a flammable liquid (Class 3) means a liquid having a flash point of not more than 60 °C (140 °F), or any material in a liquid phase with a flash point at or above 37.8 °C (100 °F) that is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging, with the following exceptions:
(1) Any liquid meeting one of the definitions specified in § 173.115.
(2) Any mixture having one or more components with a flash point of 60 °C (140 °F) or higher, that make up at least 99 percent of the total volume of the mixture, if the mixture is not offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point.
(3) Any liquid with a flash point greater than 35 °C (95 °F) that does not sustain combustion according to ASTM D 4206 (IBR, see § 171.7 of this subchapter) or the procedure in appendix H of this part.

verdict.summary:
# Compliance Determination — Transport Classification of a Liquid with Flash Point 65 °C (149 °F)

**Scope:** U.S. DOT / PHMSA hazardous materials regulations, 49 CFR Parts 171–180, domestic transport, material offered at ambient temperature in the condition described. Prepared by the Compliance Engineer.

---

## 1. Answer (verdict)

**No. The liquid is not a Class 3 flammable liquid.**

Under 49 CFR 173.120(a) a Class 3 flammable liquid is a liquid with a flash point of **not more than 60 °C (140 °F)**. This material's flash point is **65 °C (149 °F)**, which is 5 °C above the Class 3 ceiling, so it fails the defining test.

**What it is:** a **combustible liquid** under 49 CFR 173.120(b)(1) — "any liquid that does not meet the definition of any other hazard class specified in this subchapter and has a flash point above 60 °C (140 °F) and below 93 °C (200 °F)." The stated flash point (65 °C) lies strictly between 60 °C and 93 °C, and the request stipulates that the material meets no other hazard class.

**Regulatory consequence:** "combustible liquid" is a defined term, not a hazard class. Class 3 is the hazard class (49 CFR 171.8: "Class 3. See § 173.120"). A material that is only a combustible liquid does not meet the defining criteria of any hazard class in Part 173 and is therefore **not a hazardous material for transport** — provided the independent checks in §5 below all come back negative. No shipping paper, Class 3 label, placard, emergency response information, or Part 172/173 packaging authorization is required for it as such.

Two conditions must be confirmed before that conclusion is relied on: (a) the 65 °C figure is a valid **closed-cup** result from a method listed in 173.120(c)(1); and (b) the material is **not** intentionally heated and offered/transported at or above 65 °C in a bulk packaging (see §4.1).

---

## 2. Governing regulatory text (verbatim, as retrieved)

**49 CFR 173.120(a) — Flammable liquid:**
> "a flammable liquid (Class 3) means a liquid having a flash point of not more than 60 °C (140 °F), or any material in a liquid phase with a flash point at or above 37.8 °C (100 °F) that is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging, with the following exceptions: (1) Any liquid meeting one of the definitions specified in § 173.115. (2) Any mixture having one or more components with a flash point of 60 °C (140 °F) or higher, that make up at least 99 percent of the total volume of the mixture, if the mixture is not offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point. (3) Any liquid with a flash point greater than 35 °C (95 °F) that does not sustain combustion according to ASTM D 4206 … (4) Any liquid with a flash point greater than 35 °C (95 °F) and with a fire point greater than 100 °C (212 °F) according to ISO 2592 … (5) Any liquid with a flash point greater than 35 °C (95 °F) which is in a water-miscible solution with a water content of more than 90 percent by mass."

**49 CFR 173.120(b) — Combustible liquid:**
> "(1) … a combustible liquid means any liquid that does not meet the definition of any other hazard class specified in this subchapter and has a flash point above 60 °C (140 °F) and below 93 °C (200 °F). (2) A flammable liquid with a flash point at or above 38 °C (100 °F) that does not meet the definition of any other hazard class may be reclassed as a combustible liquid. This provision does not apply to transportation by vessel or aircraft, except where other means of transportation is impracticable. An elevated temperature material that meets the definition of a Class 3 material because it is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point may not be reclassed as a combustible liquid."

**49 CFR 173.120(c)(1) — Flash point determination:** closed-cup methods only — ASTM D 56 (Tag CC), ASTM D 3278 (small-scale CC), ASTM D 93 (Pensky-Martens CC), ISO 1516, ISO 1523, ISO 2719, ISO 3679, ISO 3680, ISO 13736 (Abel CC), selected by viscosity/surface-film characteristics.

**49 CFR 171.8 — Elevated temperature material:** bulk packaging and (1) liquid phase at ≥ 100 °C; or (2) liquid phase with flash point ≥ 38 °C intentionally heated and offered/transported at or above its flash point; or (3) solid phase at ≥ 240 °C.

---

## 3. Classification walk-through (decision record)

| Step | Question | Basis | Result for this material |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Is it a liquid? Melting/initial melting point ≤ 20 °C at 101.3 kPa (or fluidity per ASTM D 4359 / ADR 2.3.4 for viscous materials) | 171.8 "Liquid" | Assumed yes (a flash point determination presupposes a liquid). **Confirm on the test report.** |
| 2 | Is the 65 °C figure from an acceptable method? | 173.120(c)(1) | Must be closed cup: ASTM D 56, D 3278, D 93, or ISO 1516/1523/2719/3679/3680/13736. **Open-cup results (e.g., ASTM D 1310, Cleveland open cup) are not an acceptable basis** and are typically several degrees higher than closed cup. Assumed valid per the project assumptions. |
| 3 | Flash point ≤ 60 °C? | 173.120(a) prong 1 | **No — 65 °C > 60 °C. Fails.** Not Class 3 on this prong. |
| 4 | Elevated-temperature override: liquid phase, flash point ≥ 37.8 °C, intentionally heated, offered/transported at or above flash point, in a bulk packaging? | 173.120(a) prong 2; 171.8 | 65 °C ≥ 37.8 °C, so the flash-point condition is met; the answer turns entirely on bulk packaging + heating. **Assumed not heated, not bulk-heated → override not triggered.** See §4.1. |
| 5 | Do the 173.120(a)(1)–(5) exceptions apply? | 173.120(a)(1)–(5) | Moot. Exceptions (2)–(5) exist only to remove a material that would otherwise be Class 3; a 65 °C material never enters Class 3. (a)(1) (a Class 2 gas definition) is not implicated. Record them anyway in the file, since they show the material would remain outside Class 3 even if the flash point were lower. |
| 6 | Is it a combustible liquid? Flash point > 60 °C and < 93 °C, and no other hazard class | 173.120(b)(1) | **Yes.** 60 °C < 65 °C < 93 °C, and no other hazard class per the request. |
| 7 | Does "combustible liquid" make it a hazardous material? | 171.8 "Hazardous material"; Part 173 class definitions | **No, not by itself.** Combustible liquid is not a hazard class. Regulated only if an independent trigger in §5 applies. |
| 8 | Packing group | 173.121 | **None / not applicable** — packing groups are assigned only to Class 3 material. |

**Note on a common error:** 173.120(b)(2) (reclassing a flammable liquid with flash point ≥ 38 °C as a combustible liquid) is **not** the provision that classifies this material. (b)(2) only converts a material that is *already* Class 3. A 65 °C material is a combustible liquid under (b)(1) directly, without any reclassing election.

---

## 4. Facts that would change the answer

### 4.1 Elevated-temperature transport (the only realistic path back into Class 3)
If the material is (i) in a **bulk packaging**, (ii) **intentionally heated**, and (iii) offered for transportation or transported **at or above 65 °C**, it **is Class 3** under the second prong of 173.120(a), and is also an **elevated temperature material** under 171.8. It then may **not** be reclassed as a combustible liquid (173.120(b)(2), last sentence), and requires the Class 3 (or elevated-temperature, as applicable) shipping description, packaging, marking, and placarding. Packing group is assigned under 173.121; for a material that is Class 3 solely because it is an elevated temperature material, the practical assignment is PG III — **confirm the current 173.121 text before using it on a shipping paper.** Non-bulk packages heated above flash point do not trigger the Class 3 prong, because both 173.120(a) and the 171.8 definition require a bulk packaging.

### 4.2 Flash-point data risk
65 °C is only 5 °C above the 60 °C ceiling. Apply the repeatability/reproducibility of the method used (per the ASTM/ISO standard's precision section) to the reported result. If the lower precision bound of the result falls at or below 60 °C, the defensible call is to **classify as Class 3 (PG III) or retest**, not to rely on the single number. Record the method, apparatus, laboratory, sample identification, date, and precision statement in the classification file.

### 4.3 Sensitivity table

| If, in fact… | Then… | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| Closed-cup flash point is ≤ 60 °C | Class 3; PG III for flash point 23–60 °C with initial boiling point > 35 °C; may be reclassed as combustible under (b)(2) if flash point ≥ 38 °C and not vessel/air | 173.120(a), 173.121, 173.120(b)(2) |
| Bulk + intentionally heated to ≥ 65 °C | Class 3 (elevated temperature); no combustible reclass | 173.120(a), 171.8, 173.120(b)(2) |
| Flash point ≥ 93 °C (200 °F) | Neither Class 3 nor a combustible liquid; still screen §5 triggers | 173.120(b)(1) |
| Does not sustain combustion (ASTM D 4206 or Part 173 App. H) and flash point > 35 °C | Removed from Class 3 by (a)(3) — already outside | 173.120(a)(3) |
| Fire point > 100 °C per ISO 2592 and flash point > 35 °C | Removed from Class 3 by (a)(4) — already outside | 173.120(a)(4) |
| Water-miscible solution, > 90 % water by mass, flash point > 35 °C | Removed from Class 3 by (a)(5) — already outside | 173.120(a)(5) |
| Mixture: ≥ 99 vol % of components have flash point ≥ 60 °C, and not transported at/above flash point | Removed from Class 3 by (a)(2) — already outside | 173.120(a)(2) |
| Offered by vessel or aircraft | (b)(2) reclass unavailable; verify modal rules — but 65 °C closed cup exceeds the 60 °C Class 3 cutoff in IMDG/IATA/UN Model Regulations as well, so still not Class 3 absent heating | 173.120(b)(2); IMDG 2.3.1; IATA DGR 3.3 |

---

## 5. Independent triggers that would make it a hazardous material anyway

"Meets no other hazard class" does **not** by itself mean "not regulated." Confirm each of the following and document the result:

1. **Listed by name in the §172.101 Hazardous Materials Table.** If the material is a named substance, the HMT entry governs regardless of flash point. (The Table also contains domestic combustible-liquid entries such as "Combustible liquid, n.o.s."; verify the current entry and its conditions if a description is ever needed.)
2. **CERCLA hazardous substance** (40 CFR 302; 49 CFR 172.101 Appendix A) — regulated as a hazardous material when shipped in one package at or above its reportable quantity.
3. **Marine pollutant** (49 CFR 172.101 Appendix B; 171.8) — triggers marking and shipping-paper requirements under the HMR independent of mode.
4. **Hazardous waste** (40 CFR 261; 171.8) — a hazardous waste is a hazardous material regardless of its physical/flammability characteristics.
5. **Elevated temperature material** (171.8) — bulk + ≥ 100 °C liquid, or bulk + flash point ≥ 38 °C heated to/above flash point, or bulk + solid ≥ 240 °C.
6. **Any other hazard class** — verify the "no other class" assertion against Classes 1–9, not just flammability: pH/corrosivity (Class 8), acute toxicity (Class 6.1), oxidizing/combustion-supporting behavior (Class 5.1), self-heating (Class 4.2), etc.

If all six are negative, the material is not subject to the HMR.

---

## 6. Documentation package for the classification file

1. Flash point test report — method from 173.120(c)(1), closed cup, apparatus, lab, sample ID, date, result 65 °C, and the method's precision statement.
2. Melting point / fluidity determination supporting the "liquid" definition (171.8).
3. Composition and hazard-class screening memo covering Classes 1–9.
4. Statement of the offering condition: ambient temperature, packaging type (non-bulk vs bulk), and confirmation that the material is not intentionally heated to or above 65 °C in a bulk packaging.
5. Appendix A (CERCLA) and Appendix B (marine pollutant) screens; hazardous-waste determination if applicable.
6. Written classification determination signed and dated, stating: "Flash point 65 °C closed cup (method ___). Not a Class 3 flammable liquid per 49 CFR 173.120(a); combustible liquid per 49 CFR 173.120(b)(1); not subject to the HMR as a hazardous material."
7. Re-evaluation trigger: any change in formulation, supplier, test method, or offering temperature requires re-determination.

---

## 7. What goes on the documents

- **Shipping paper:** none required; no proper shipping name, hazard class, UN number, or emergency response telephone number is mandated. A carrier-required notation is acceptable and common, e.g. "Not regulated — combustible liquid, flash point 65 °C (149 °F) closed cup." Do **not** apply a Class 3 label, a Class 3 hazard class designation, or placards.
- **SDS Section 14:** "US DOT: Not regulated as a hazardous material (combustible liquid, flash point 65 °C / 149 °F closed cup; above the 60 °C Class 3 threshold)." This is *not* inconsistent with Section 2 — the two regimes use different cutoffs; say so explicitly in the SDS to preempt auditor questions.

---

## 8. Adjacent regimes (the SDS will classify it differently — this is expected)

| Regime | Classification at flash point 65 °C (149 °F) | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| US DOT transport (49 CFR) | Combustible liquid; not a Class 3 flammable liquid; not regulated as a hazardous material absent §5 triggers | 173.120(a), (b)(1) |
| OSHA HazCom / GHS | **Flammable liquid, Category 4** (flash point > 60 °C and ≤ 93 °C); H227 "Combustible liquid"; no pictogram, no signal word | 29 CFR 1910.1200 App. B / GHS criteria |
| NFPA 30 / 29 CFR 1910.106 | **Class IIIA combustible liquid** (≥ 140 °F and < 200 °F) | 1910.106(a)(18) |
| IMDG / IATA / UN Model Regs | Not Class 3 (above 60 °C closed cup) unless transported at or above its flash point | IMDG 2.3.1; IATA DGR 3.3 |
| EPA | RCRA hazardous waste if discarded; CERCLA release reporting if listed; storage/SPCC programs per facility applicability | 40 CFR 261, 302 |

---

## 9. Bottom line

Not Class 3. It is a **combustible liquid** under 49 CFR 173.120(b)(1), and — subject to the closed-cup data being valid, the material not being bulk-heated to or above its flash point, and the §5 screens being negative — it is **not subject to the Hazardous Materials Regulations** for domestic transport. Document the closed-cup result, the ambient/non-bulk-heated offering condition, and the CERCLA/marine-pollutant/hazardous-waste/HMT screens in the classification file, and re-determine if the formulation, the test method, or the offering temperature changes.

quotes.whole:
§ 20.1301 Dose limits for individual members of the public.




(a) Each licensee shall conduct operations so that—




(1) The total effective dose equivalent to individual members of the public from the licensed operation does not exceed 0.1 rem (1 mSv) in a year, exclusive of the dose contributions from background radiation, from any medical administration the individual has received, from exposure to individuals administered radioactive material and released under § 35.75, from voluntary participation in medical research programs, and from the licensee's disposal of radioactive material into sanitary sewerage in accordance with § 20.2003, and






(2) The dose in any unrestricted area from external sources, exclusive of the dose contributions from patients administered radioactive material and released in accordance with § 35.75, does not exceed 0.002 rem (0.02 millisievert) in any one hour.








(b) If the licensee permits members of the public to have access to controlled areas, the limits for members of the public continue to apply to those individuals.






(c) Notwithstanding paragraph (a)(1) of this section, a licensee may permit visitors to an individual who cannot be released, under § 35.75, to receive a radiation dose greater than 0.1 rem (1 mSv) if—




(1) The radiation dose received does not exceed 0.5 rem (5 mSv); and






(2) The authorized user, as defined in 10 CFR Part 35, has determined before the visit that it is appropriate.








(d) A licensee or license applicant may apply for prior NRC authorization to operate up to an annual dose limit for an individual member of the public of 0.5 rem (5 mSv). The licensee or license applicant shall include the following information in this application:




(1) Demonstration of the need for and the expected duration of operations in excess of the limit in paragraph (a) of this section;






(2) The licensee's program to assess and control dose within the 0.5 rem (5 mSv) annual limit; and






(3) The procedures to be followed to maintain the dose as low as is reasonably achievable.








(e) In addition to the requirements of this part, a licensee subject to the provisions of EPA's generally applicable environmental radiation standards in 40 CFR part 190 shall comply with those standards.





(f) The Commission may impose additional restrictions on radiation levels in unrestricted areas and on the total quantity of radionuclides that a licensee may release in effluents in order to restrict the collective dose.



[56 FR 23398, May 21, 1991, as amended at 60 FR 48625, Sept. 20, 1995; 62 FR 4133, Jan. 29, 1997; 67 FR 20370, Apr. 24, 2002; 67 FR 62872, Oct. 9, 2002]

verdict.summary:
# NRC public dose limits — annual and any-one-hour, unrestricted area

## 1. Answer at a glance

| # | Limit | Citation | Quantity | Value (US) | Value (SI) |
|---|-------|----------|----------|-----------|-----------|
| **A** | **Annual public dose limit** | **10 CFR 20.1301(a)(1)** | Total effective dose equivalent (TEDE), all pathways, from the licensed operation | **0.1 rem in a year** (100 mrem/yr) | **1 mSv/yr** |
| **B** | **Any-one-hour limit in an unrestricted area** | **10 CFR 20.1301(a)(2)** | Dose **from external sources** in any unrestricted area | **0.002 rem in any one hour** (2 mrem/h) | **0.02 mSv (20 µSv) in any one hour** |

The directly asked figure — *any one hour in an unrestricted area* — is **0.002 rem per hour (0.02 mSv/h; 2 mrem/h; 20 µSv/h)**. The companion annual figure is **0.1 rem (1 mSv) per year** TEDE.

These are two independent limits. Both must be satisfied simultaneously; neither is a proration of the other.

## 2. Verbatim regulatory text

10 CFR 20.1301 (Subpart D — Radiation Dose Limits for Individual Members of the Public), paragraphs (a) and (b):

> **§ 20.1301 Dose limits for individual members of the public.**
>
> (a) Each licensee shall conduct operations so that—
>
> (1) The total effective dose equivalent to individual members of the public from the licensed operation does not exceed 0.1 rem (1 mSv) in a year, exclusive of the dose contributions from background radiation, from any medical administration the individual has received, from exposure to individuals administered radioactive material and released under § 35.75, from voluntary participation in medical research programs, and from the licensee's disposal of radioactive material into sanitary sewerage in accordance with § 20.2003, and
>
> (2) The dose in any unrestricted area from external sources, exclusive of the dose contributions from patients administered radioactive material and released in accordance with § 35.75, does not exceed 0.002 rem (0.02 millisievert) in any one hour.
>
> (b) If the licensee permits members of the public to have access to controlled areas, the limits for members of the public continue to apply to those individuals.

Source history: 56 FR 23398, May 21, 1991; amended at 60 FR 48625 (Sept. 20, 1995); 62 FR 4133 (Jan. 29, 1997); 67 FR 20370 (Apr. 24, 2002); 67 FR 62872 (Oct. 9, 2002). Text above is the current eCFR text and matches the 2025 printed CFR (10 CFR Ch. I, 1–1–25 Edition, p. 358).

## 3. Scope difference between the two limits — the point most often gotten wrong

| | Annual limit, (a)(1) | Hourly limit, (a)(2) |
|---|---|---|
| Dose quantity | TEDE (external + committed effective dose equivalent from inhalation/ingestion) | Dose from **external sources only** |
| Pathway coverage | All pathways from the licensed operation, including effluent releases | Direct external exposure (gamma, x-ray, beta, neutron) only |
| Where it applies | To the **individual** member of the public (the maximally exposed individual) | To the **area** — any unrestricted area, whether or not anyone is present |
| Time basis | Calendar year | Any single clock hour; **no averaging over a year is permitted** |
| Occupancy assumption | Actual/assumed occupancy of the maximally exposed individual | Evaluated as if an individual were present for that hour |

Consequences to state plainly to a licensee:

- There is **no one-hour limit for internal dose**. Short-term control of internal dose is achieved indirectly, through the annual-average effluent concentration limits of appendix B, table 2 (see §20.1302(b)(2)(i)) and through ALARA.
- The hourly limit is an **area** limit and is not satisfied by controlling access. If the dose rate anywhere in an unrestricted area exceeds 2 mrem/h (20 µSv/h), the licensee is out of compliance even if no one is there. The remedy is shielding, distance, source relocation, or reclassifying the area as controlled (with the access controls that implies) — not a sign or an administrative control alone.
- Conversely, meeting 2 mrem/h everywhere does **not** demonstrate compliance with the annual limit; a location at exactly 2 mrem/h occupied continuously would yield ~17.5 rem/yr (0.002 rem/h × 8,766 h = 17.53 rem = 175 mSv), seventeen times the annual limit. This is precisely why the two limits coexist: the annual limit governs chronic low-level exposure, the hourly limit catches localized high dose rates (shielded-source failures, hot spots, mispositioned sources, collimator or cask leakage).

## 4. Exclusions and inclusions

**Excluded from the annual 0.1 rem (1 mSv) limit** — these dose contributions are not counted against the licensee:

1. Background radiation.
2. Any medical administration the individual has received (diagnostic or therapeutic).
3. Exposure to individuals administered radioactive material and released under §35.75 (i.e., released patients are not the licensee's dose burden).
4. Voluntary participation in medical research programs.
5. The licensee's disposal of radioactive material into sanitary sewerage in accordance with §20.2003.

**Excluded from the hourly 0.002 rem limit**: dose contributions from patients administered radioactive material and released in accordance with §35.75. (Note the asymmetry — the hourly exclusion list is narrower; background is not expressly listed in (a)(2), but the limit is on dose *from the licensed operation* and natural background is not a licensee contribution.)

**Included**: dose to members of the public who are permitted access to controlled areas — §20.1301(b) keeps the public limits applicable to those individuals.

## 5. Exceptions and alternate limits (do not confuse these with the default)

| Provision | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| §20.1301(c) — visitors to a patient who cannot be released under §35.75 | Up to **0.5 rem (5 mSv)** | Only for visitors of such a patient; the authorized user (10 CFR Part 35) must determine **before the visit** that it is appropriate. This is a per-visit authorization, not a standing annual allowance. |
| §20.1301(d) — alternate annual limit | Up to **0.5 rem (5 mSv) per year** | Requires **prior NRC authorization**; application must contain (1) demonstration of need and expected duration of operations above the 0.1 rem limit, (2) the program to assess and control dose within the 0.5 rem limit, and (3) procedures to maintain dose ALARA. This is the only route by which the annual public limit may lawfully be exceeded; it does not exist as an as-of-right option. |
| §20.1301(e) | — | A licensee also subject to EPA's generally applicable environmental radiation standards in 40 CFR part 190 must comply with those as well. |
| §20.1301(f) | — | The Commission may impose additional restrictions on radiation levels in unrestricted areas and on total radionuclide quantities released, to restrict collective dose. |

**Important:** there is no provision anywhere in Part 20 that permits averaging the 0.002 rem/h limit over a year, over a day, or over a shift. The 0.5 rem/yr figure in (d) is an *annual* alternative and does not relax (a)(2); a licensee operating under (d) is still bound by 0.002 rem in any one hour.

## 6. How compliance is demonstrated — §20.1302

§20.1302(a): the licensee must make surveys of radiation levels in unrestricted and controlled areas and of radioactive materials in effluents released to those areas, to demonstrate compliance with §20.1301.

§20.1302(b) offers two compliance routes for the annual limit:

- **(b)(1)** Demonstrate by measurement or calculation that the TEDE to the individual likely to receive the highest dose from the licensed operation does not exceed the annual limit (the maximally exposed individual / MEI approach); **or**
- **(b)(2)** Demonstrate both of the following:
  - (i) annual average concentrations of radioactive material in gaseous and liquid effluents at the unrestricted-area boundary do not exceed appendix B, table 2 values; **and**
  - (ii) **if an individual were continuously present in an unrestricted area**, the dose from external sources would not exceed **0.002 rem (0.02 mSv) in an hour and 0.05 rem (0.5 mSv) in a year**.

Two practical notes for the one-hour figure:

- A calibrated survey instrument reading of **2 mrem/h (20 µSv/h)** at the unrestricted-area boundary is the compliance boundary. A reading at or below 2 mrem/h, sustained for the full hour, meets (a)(2); anything above it is a violation in that hour regardless of duration.
- The (b)(2)(ii) external-only annual figure of **0.05 rem (0.5 mSv)** is exactly half the 0.1 rem TEDE limit — the other half is implicitly reserved for the internal (inhalation/ingestion) pathway. 0.05 rem/yr ÷ 8,766 h = **5.7 µrem/h (0.057 µSv/h)**, which is far below 2 mrem/h, so for continuous occupancy the annual external criterion governs and the hourly limit is not the binding constraint.

## 7. Definitions that fix the scope (10 CFR 20.1003)

- **Unrestricted area** — an area to which access is neither limited by the licensee for purposes of protecting individuals from exposure to radiation and radioactive materials, nor any area used for residential quarters. (Paraphrase of §20.1003; consult the current definitional text for exact wording when drafting.)
- **Member of the public** — any individual, except when that individual is receiving an occupational dose. Occupational dose is governed by Subpart C (§§20.1201–20.1208: 5 rem/yr TEDE, etc.), not by §20.1301. This is the dividing line: the same person can be an occupationally exposed worker on site and a member of the public off site, but not both for the same exposure.
- **Total effective dose equivalent (TEDE)** — the sum of the deep-dose equivalent (external) and the committed effective dose equivalent (internal), as defined in §20.1003.

## 8. Related but distinct limits (context, not answers to the question)

These are frequently conflated with §20.1301 in licensee discussions. They are separate requirements:

- **ALARA, §20.1101(b)** — the licensee must make every reasonable effort to maintain public and occupational doses ALARA, i.e., well below the §20.1301 limits. ALARA is an obligation on the licensee, not a numerical public limit.
- **Air-emission constraint, §20.1101(d)** — a 10 mrem/yr (0.1 mSv/yr) constraint on radionuclide emissions to ambient air for the licensees to which that paragraph applies (the 40 CFR part 61, subpart I interface). Confirm the current applicability conditions before citing it in a licensing document.
- **Effluent concentration limits, appendix B, table 2 to Part 20** — annual-average concentration limits at the unrestricted-area boundary; used as a compliance route under §20.1302(b)(2)(i).
- **EPA fuel-cycle standards, 40 CFR part 190** — 25 mrem/yr whole-body TEDE, 75 mrem/yr thyroid, 25 mrem/yr any other organ, for the uranium fuel cycle; incorporated by §20.1301(e).
- **EPA NESHAP, 40 CFR part 61, subpart I** — 10 mrem/yr effective dose and 3 mrem/yr iodine-131, for designated facilities.

## 9. Jurisdiction and applicability

- The limits above are those of the **U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission** under **10 CFR Part 20**, the NRC's primary radiation-protection rule.
- **Agreement States** adopt compatible regulations under their own citations; the numerical limits are, in practice, the same (typically 0.1 rem/yr and 0.002 rem/h), but the citable authority in an Agreement State is the State regulation, not 10 CFR 20.1301.
- §20.1301 applies to **NRC licensees** (and to persons holding a license or applying for one, per (d)). It does not set limits for background, for medical exposure of patients (that is a Part 35 / FDA matter), or for non-licensed sources.

## 10. Assumptions made in answering (correct these if they are wrong for your use)

1. The requester wants the limits as stated in **10 CFR Part 20, Subpart D**, current as of the eCFR text retrieved 2026-11-17 — not another framework (e.g., DOE Order 458.1, which sets 100 mrem/yr for DOE operations, or ICRP recommendations).
2. "Dose" for the annual limit means **TEDE**; "dose" for the hourly limit means **dose from external sources**.
3. "Unrestricted area" is used in the §20.1003 sense, and the question is the general regulatory-knowledge question, not a specific licensee's licensing basis.
4. NRC jurisdiction (not Agreement State, not another federal agency).
5. The requester wants the **regulatory limits themselves**, not licensee-set dose constraints or NRC guidance values (e.g., the lower administrative constraint values found in some license conditions).

## 11. Bottom line for a one-line citation

> Under 10 CFR 20.1301(a), an NRC licensee must conduct operations so that (1) the total effective dose equivalent to individual members of the public does not exceed **0.1 rem (1 mSv) in a year**, and (2) the dose in any unrestricted area from external sources does not exceed **0.002 rem (0.02 mSv; 2 mrem; 20 µSv) in any one hour**.

verdict.summary:
# Compliance Determination — Alcohol Concentration Bar for US CMV Drivers

## 1. Determination (the answer)

A driver of a commercial motor vehicle is barred from reporting for duty or remaining on duty requiring the performance of safety-sensitive functions at an **alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater**.

The threshold is **inclusive**: 0.04 itself bars duty. The unit of measure under the federal program is **grams of alcohol per 210 liters of breath (g/210 L BrAC)**, as indicated by an evidential breath test conducted under 49 CFR Part 40.

- Controlling authority: **49 CFR § 382.201 (Alcohol concentration)**, Part 382, Subpart B (Prohibitions), FMCSA.
- Current text (eCFR, verified):

> § 382.201 Alcohol concentration.
> No driver shall report for duty or remain on duty requiring the performance of safety-sensitive functions while having an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater. No employer having knowledge that a driver has an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater shall permit the driver to perform or continue to perform safety-sensitive functions.
> [66 FR 43103, Aug. 17, 2001, as amended at 77 FR 4483, Jan. 30, 2012]

The rule is bilateral: it prohibits the **driver** from reporting/remaining on duty, and separately prohibits the **employer** from permitting the driver to perform or continue to perform safety-sensitive functions once the employer has knowledge of a 0.04-or-greater result. (The 2012 amendment at 77 FR 4483 changed the employer standard in § 382.201 from "actual knowledge" to "knowledge"; § 382.205 and § 382.207 retain "actual knowledge" language.)

## 2. Measurement basis and definition

"Alcohol concentration" (or "alcohol content") is defined in **49 CFR § 382.107** and **49 CFR § 40.3** as the alcohol in a volume of breath expressed in terms of grams of alcohol per 210 liters of breath as indicated by an evidential breath test under the rule. Practical consequences of that definition:

1. The federal program's operative measurement is **breath**, taken on an evidential breath testing device (EBT) that appears on the ODAPC conforming-products list and meets Part 40 calibration/maintenance requirements.
2. **Blood test results are not DOT test results.** A hospital or law-enforcement blood draw may support a state criminal case or an employer's independent action, but it does not establish a § 382.201 violation for purposes of the DOT program. Do not convert a blood result into a breath figure and treat it as a DOT test result.
3. A 0.04 BrAC corresponds to a whole-blood alcohol concentration of roughly 0.04 g/dL under the standard 2100:1 breath-to-blood partition ratio, but the federal bar is expressed and enforced in breath units.

## 3. Threshold table — do not conflate these

| Result (BrAC) | Regulatory characterization | Required action |
|---|---|---|
| 0.00 – 0.019 | Negative / below all thresholds | No action; driver may perform safety-sensitive functions (subject to §§ 382.205, 382.207, 382.209 below). |
| 0.02 – 0.039 | **Not** a § 382.201 violation, but a removal trigger under § 382.505 (Subpart E) | Driver may not perform or continue safety-sensitive functions until the return-to-duty process in § 382.503 is completed (SAP evaluation, return-to-duty test < 0.02, follow-up testing). |
| **0.04 or greater** | **Violation of § 382.201** — the bar asked about | Immediate removal from safety-sensitive functions; SAP referral under § 382.501(c); no return until § 382.503 process complete. |

Note on the 0.02 line: 0.02 is a **testing/removal** threshold, not the answer to the question posed. It is lower than 0.04 and does not modify it. The 0.04 figure is the concentration at which the driver is barred by the prohibition itself.

## 4. How a result is established (Part 40 procedure)

1. **Screening test** on an approved alcohol screening device or EBT. A screening result of **0.02 or greater** requires a **confirmation test**; a screening result below 0.02 is treated as negative.
2. **Confirmation test** on an EBT, administered after the required waiting period (at least 15 minutes, and no more than 30 minutes, after the screening test) and without any substance ingested in the interim.
3. **The confirmation test result is the result of record.** A screening result alone never supports a § 382.201 violation.
4. Tests must be conducted by a trained BAT/STT under 49 CFR Part 40, Subpart J (alcohol testing), with the alcohol testing form (ATF) completed; the driver's CDL number and State of issuance are recorded per § 382.403(b).
5. **Refusal to test** is treated as a violation equivalent to a 0.04-or-greater result (§ 382.211) and triggers the same removal and SAP process.

## 5. Bars that operate independently of concentration

These prohibit safety-sensitive duty regardless of any measured concentration and should not be read as lowering the numeric threshold:

- **§ 382.205 — On-duty use.** No driver may use alcohol while performing safety-sensitive functions.
- **§ 382.207 — Pre-duty use.** No driver may perform safety-sensitive functions **within four hours after using alcohol**.
- **§ 382.209 — Use following an accident.** A driver required to take a post-accident alcohol test may not use alcohol for **eight hours** following the accident, or until an alcohol test is administered, whichever occurs first.
- **§ 382.211 — Refusal to submit** to a required test.
- **§ 382.213 / § 382.215 — Controlled substance use**, including Schedule I drugs and non-Schedule I drugs outside a licensed practitioner's instruction.

A driver who has consumed any alcohol within four hours is barred even at a measured concentration of 0.00. Compliance programs must therefore enforce the timing rules and the 0.04 line as separate controls.

## 6. Employer obligations and consequences of a ≥ 0.04 result

1. **Remove** the driver from safety-sensitive functions immediately — including driving — and do not permit performance or continued performance (§ 382.201, § 382.501).
2. **Refer** the driver to a **Substance Abuse Professional** (§ 382.501(c)); the SAP performs the evaluation and prescribes education/treatment.
3. **Return-to-duty** only after the SAP process is complete and the driver passes a **return-to-duty alcohol test with a result of less than 0.02** (§ 382.309), conducted under direct observation.
4. **Follow-up testing** as prescribed by the SAP: at least **six** tests in the first **twelve** months of return to duty, and continuation for up to **60 months** (§ 382.311), with alcohol follow-up tests under direct observation.
5. **Recordkeeping**: alcohol test records are maintained under § 382.401; violation and return-to-duty information is reported to and queried from the **FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse** (§ 382.601–382.609 series, including the CDL-holder consent and query requirements).
6. **Driver education materials** must be distributed under § 382.601, describing the 0.04 prohibition and the consequences.
7. **Testing program context** (not thresholds): random alcohol testing at a minimum annual rate of **10%** of average driver positions and random controlled-substances testing at **50%** (§ 382.305); post-accident alcohol testing attempted within **8 hours** of the accident, with attempts ceasing and documentation made if not administered within that window (§ 382.303); pre-employment alcohol testing is optional, but if conducted must follow Part 40 (§ 382.301(c)).

## 7. Interaction with state law

Many states impose their own CMV alcohol limits and penalties (some at 0.04, some at 0.02, plus separate "implied consent" and criminal provisions). The **federal** bar under Part 382 is 0.04. Part 382 preempts state or local requirements that are inconsistent with or that impose additional testing requirements on employers covered by Part 382 (§ 382.109), but state criminal law, licensing sanctions, and out-of-service criteria applied by enforcement officers operate independently of the federal testing program. A state limit below 0.04 does not change the answer to this question; it changes the driver's exposure to state penalties.

## 8. Audit / verification checklist

- [ ] Written policy states the **0.04 or greater** prohibition verbatim in substance, and separately states the 0.02 removal rule.
- [ ] Policy states the four-hour pre-duty rule and the eight-hour post-accident rule as independent bars.
- [ ] Supervisors trained on reasonable-suspicion testing (§ 382.307) and on the immediate-removal duty.
- [ ] Only EBTs on the ODAPC conforming-products list are used; calibration and BAT training records current.
- [ ] Confirmation test performed and its result — not the screening result — recorded as the result of record.
- [ ] SAP referral, return-to-duty test result **< 0.02**, and follow-up testing schedule documented in the driver's file.
- [ ] Clearinghouse query/reporting obligations satisfied for any § 382.201 violation.

## 9. Common errors this determination corrects

1. Answering **0.02** — that is the confirmation-testing and removal threshold under § 382.505, not the § 382.201 prohibition.
2. Answering **0.08** — the common state DUI per-se limit; it does not govern CMV drivers under Part 382.
3. Treating 0.04 as exclusive ("more than 0.04") — the regulation says "0.04 **or greater**."
4. Using a blood test result as the DOT result — the federal program is a breath-test program.
5. Believing a driver under 0.04 is always clear to drive — the four-hour pre-duty rule, the on-duty-use rule, and the eight-hour post-accident rule bar duty regardless of concentration.

## 10. Sources

- 49 CFR § 382.201, eCFR (current): https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-III/subchapter-B/part-382/subpart-B/section-382.201
- 49 CFR Part 382, GovInfo CFR 2022 compilations (§§ 382.201, 382.205, 382.207, 382.209): https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2022-title49-vol5/pdf/CFR-2022-title49-vol5-part382.pdf
- 49 CFR Part 382, GovInfo CFR 2023 compilation (§§ 382.201, 382.211, 382.213): https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2023-title49-vol5/pdf/CFR-2023-title49-vol5-sec382-207.pdf
- 49 CFR § 382.201, GovInfo CFR 2006 XML (historical continuity of the 0.04 threshold): https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2006-title49-vol5/xml/CFR-2006-title49-vol5-sec382-201.xml
- Related provisions cited by section number: 49 CFR §§ 382.107 (definitions), 382.109 (preemption), 382.211, 382.301, 382.303, 382.305, 382.307, 382.309, 382.311, 382.401, 382.403, 382.501, 382.503, 382.505, 382.601; 49 CFR Part 40, Subpart J (alcohol testing procedures) and § 40.3 (definitions).

**Bottom line: 0.04 g/210 L breath, inclusive — a CMV driver may not report for or remain on duty requiring safety-sensitive functions at an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater (49 CFR § 382.201).**

quotes.whole:
Entitlement
Almost all people classed as workers are legally entitled to 5.6 weeks’ paid holiday a year (known as statutory leave entitlement or annual leave).
This includes:
agency workers
workers with ‘irregular hours’ (where the number of hours they work in a pay period often or always changes)
‘part-year’ workers (where there are periods of at least a week in a leave year where they do not need to work and are not paid)
An employer can include bank holidays as part of statutory annual leave.
Statutory annual leave entitlement
Most workers who work a 5-day week must receive at least 28 days’ paid annual leave a year. This is the equivalent of 5.6 weeks of holiday.
Working part-time
Part-time workers who work regular hours for the whole year are entitled to at least 5.6 weeks’ paid holiday, but this will amount to fewer than 28 days.
For example, if they work 3 days a week, they must get at least 16.8 days’ leave a year (3 × 5.6).
Use the holiday entitlement calculator to work out a part-time worker’s leave.
Working irregular hours or for part of the year
People working irregular hours or part of the year are entitled to up to 5.6 weeks statutory leave.

quotes.whole:
2. 1. Calculating leave for a full leave year
Workers who have regular working hours and a fixed length of working day should have their holiday calculated in days. This is the most straightforward calculation.
Workers who are in employment for a full leave year are entitled to 5.6 weeks’ statutory leave subject to a cap of 28 days. In practice, this cap only affects a worker if they work for more than 5 days a week.
See Calculating leave for somebody starting part way through a leave year for how workers may accrue leave when they are in the first 12 months of a job.
2.1 Days per week
The statutory holiday entitlement for a worker who works a full leave year is the lower of:
a) 28 days; or
b) 5.6 x days worked per week
Example 1
Andrew works 4 days per week, with each day being 8 hours long. His statutory leave entitlement is the lower of 28 days or 5.6 x 4 days per week, which is 22.4 days.
Therefore, Andrew’s statutory leave entitlement is 22.4 days.
Example 2
Beckie works 6 days per week. Her statutory leave entitlement is the lower of 28 days or 5.6 x 6 days per week which is 33.6 days.
Therefore, Beckie’s statutory leave entitlement is 28.0 days.

verdict.summary:
# Statutory paid annual leave — Great Britain

## Answer

| Item | Figure |
|---|---|
| Statutory minimum paid annual leave | **5.6 weeks** per leave year |
| Statutory cap on that entitlement | **28 days** |

For the standard five-day week the two figures coincide: 5.6 × 5 = 28 days. The cap is an absolute ceiling on the statutory entitlement, so it only reduces the weeks' worth of leave for someone working more than five days a week (e.g. a six-day week: 5.6 × 6 = 33.6, cut to 28 days, i.e. 4.67 weeks' worth).

## Legal basis

- **Working Time Regulations 1998 (SI 1998/1833), reg 13(1):** a worker is entitled to **4 weeks'** annual leave in each leave year (as substituted by SI 2001/3256).
- **Reg 13A(2)(e):** for any leave year beginning on or after 1 April 2009, a worker is entitled to a further **1.6 weeks'** additional annual leave (introduced by SI 2007/2079).
- **Reg 13A(3):** "The aggregate entitlement provided for in paragraph (2) and regulation 13(1) is subject to a maximum of **28 days**."
- **Arithmetic:** 4 weeks + 1.6 weeks = **5.6 weeks**; 5.6 × 5 days = **28 days**.
- **GOV.UK confirms** the same: "Almost all people classed as workers are legally entitled to 5.6 weeks' paid holiday a year"; "Most workers who work a 5-day week must receive at least 28 days' paid annual leave a year"; "Statutory paid holiday entitlement is limited to 28 days."

## Scope and interpretation

1. **"Worker".** The WTR definition covers employees and limb (b) workers — agency workers, zero-hours workers, workers with irregular hours, and part-year workers are all within the 5.6 weeks. If the questioner meant only "employee", the answer is unchanged, because every employee is a worker for these purposes.
2. **Great Britain.** England, Wales and Scotland. Northern Ireland has its own Working Time Regulations (Northern Ireland) 1998; the headline figures are the same but NI is outside the scope of this answer. The agriculture provisions in reg 13(4) and Schedule 2 (Wales/Scotland) and the Agricultural Wages (Scotland) Act 1949 carve-out in reg 13A(8) affect how leave is set for those workers, not the 5.6-week/28-day baseline for workers generally.
3. **Statutory minimum only.** 5.6 weeks is a floor. Contracts commonly give more (e.g. 25 days plus bank holidays); that extra leave is contractual and is not governed by the WTR rules on carry-over, pay and remedy. Check the contract first.
4. **Bank holidays.** There is no statutory right to bank or public holidays off. An employer may count bank holidays towards the 28 days, so a worker given "20 days plus 8 bank holidays" receives exactly the 28-day statutory minimum and nothing more.
5. **Leave year.** Reg 13(3): the leave year begins on the date set by a relevant agreement, or (absent agreement) on the anniversary of the employment start date (1 October 1998 for employment beginning on or before that date). The definition affects accrual and timing, not the 5.6-week/28-day figures.
6. **2024 amendment.** The Employment Rights (Amendment, Revocation and Transitional Provision) Regulations 2023 (SI 2023/1426) inserted reg 13(A1) and reg 15B. For leave years beginning on or after 1 April 2024, irregular-hours and part-year workers accrue leave at 12.07% of hours worked (with rolled-up holiday pay permitted), but the entitlement remains 5.6 weeks subject to the 28-day cap. For other workers, reg 13 and 13A apply as before.

## Calculation rule

For a worker with regular hours and fixed-length days, full leave year:

> **Statutory entitlement (days) = the lower of (a) 28 days, or (b) 5.6 × days worked per week.**

Worked examples:

| Days worked per week | 5.6 × days | Entitlement | Equivalent weeks |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 28.0 | 28.0 days | 5.6 weeks |
| 4 | 22.4 | 22.4 days | 5.6 weeks |
| 3 | 16.8 | 16.8 days | 5.6 weeks |
| 6 | 33.6 | **28.0 days** (cap applies) | 4.67 weeks |

- Part-time workers working regular hours all year get 5.6 weeks, which is fewer than 28 days.
- Shift workers: 5.6 weeks of the average working week, capped at 28 days' worth of shifts.
- Irregular-hours and part-year workers: from 1 April 2024, 12.07% of hours worked in the pay period, subject to the same 28-day ceiling.
- Starting or leaving part-way through a leave year: entitlement accrues pro rata (1/12 of the annual entitlement per month, or 12.07% of hours for irregular-hours workers).

## Practical HR notes

- **Holiday pay** (reg 16) must be at the worker's normal remuneration rate — regular overtime, commission and allowances that are normally paid should be reflected; the 5.6 weeks is leave, and it must be paid leave to count.
- **Record-keeping:** employers must keep records sufficient to show compliance (reg 9); this is the evidence base if entitlement is challenged.
- **Carry-over:** 4 weeks of the 5.6 (the reg 13(1) EU-derived element) can carry over where the worker could not take it because of sick leave (18 months) or because the employer failed to recognise the right, encourage leave or warn of loss; the additional 1.6 weeks carries over only if a relevant agreement so provides.
- **Do not pay in lieu** of the 5.6 weeks except on termination (reg 13A(6) and reg 14).
- **Enforcement:** Employment Tribunal claim for the reg 30 remedy; HSE/local authority for the wider WTR.

## Bottom line for the worker

Every worker in Great Britain is entitled by statute to **5.6 weeks'** paid annual leave per leave year, and that entitlement is capped at **28 days**, which is exactly what 5.6 weeks amounts to for a five-day-week worker.

document are to be interpreted as described in [RFC2119].
2.  Case Insensitivity of DNS Labels
DNS was specified in the era of [ASCII].  DNS names were expected to
look like most host names or Internet email address right halves (the
part after the at-sign, "@") or to be numeric, as in the in-addr.arpa
part of the DNS name space.  For example,
foo.example.net.
aol.com.
www.gnu.ai.mit.edu.
or  69.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa.
Case-varied alternatives to the above [RFC3092] would be DNS names
like
Foo.ExamplE.net.
AOL.COM.
WWW.gnu.AI.mit.EDU.
or  69.2.0.192.in-ADDR.ARPA.
However, the individual octets of which DNS names consist are not
limited to valid ASCII character codes.  They are 8-bit bytes, and
all values are allowed.  Many applications, however, interpret them
as ASCII characters.
2.1.  Escaping Unusual DNS Label Octets
In Master Files [STD13] and other human-readable and -writable ASCII
contexts, an escape is needed for the byte value for period (0x2E,
".") and all octet values outside of the inclusive range from 0x21
("!") to 0x7E ("~").  That is to say, 0x2E and all octet values in
the two inclusive ranges from 0x00 to 0x20 and from 0x7F to 0xFF.

lookup for DNS queries should be case insensitive [STD13].  That is
to say, a lookup string octet with a value in the inclusive range
from 0x41 to 0x5A, the uppercase ASCII letters, MUST match the
identical value and also match the corresponding value in the
inclusive range from 0x61 to 0x7A, the lowercase ASCII letters.  A
lookup string octet with a lowercase ASCII letter value MUST
similarly match the identical value and also match the corresponding
value in the uppercase ASCII letter range.

verdict.summary:
## Scope

I read 'the original DNS specification' as RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 as originally published. The numeric wire-format limits are in RFC 1035. No implementation-specific or later-RFC limit is being reported.

## Answer

| Object | Maximum | What is counted |
|---|---:|---|
| Single label | 63 octets | Label data only; the length prefix is not part of the label. |
| Encoded label field | 64 octets | 1 length octet plus up to 63 data octets. |
| Full domain name | 255 octets | Uncompressed wire encoding: all label length octets, all label data octets, and the final zero octet for the root. |

A label is not 64 octets; 64 is the on-the-wire field size. The label length octet uses its low six bits, so its literal-label range is 0 through 63. The high-order two bits must be 00 for a literal label. A length of 0 is the root label and is used only as the terminating null label.

## Specification text

RFC 1035 Section 2.3.4 ('Size limits') lists:

- labels: 63 octets or less
- names: 255 octets or less

RFC 1035 Section 3.1 says:

> The high order two bits of every length octet must be zero, and the remaining six bits of the length field limit the label to 63 octets or less.

> The total length of a domain name (i.e., label octets and label length octets) is restricted to 255 octets or less.

RFC 4343 Section 3.1 corroborates the label bound:

> ASCII labels, with a length from zero to 63 octets ... (The ASCII label of length zero is reserved for use as the name of the root node of the name tree.)

## Counting formula and checks

For a name with n labels of data lengths L1 through Ln:

    wire length = sum(1 + Li) + 1 <= 255, with 0 <= Li <= 63

The final +1 is the zero length octet of the root.

- Maximum single label: L = 63 octets. Its encoded field is 64 octets. A one-label name is 1 + 63 + 1 = 65 octets, so the label bound binds before the name bound.
- Maximum name using 63-octet labels: three labels of 63 and one of 61: (1+63)*3 + (1+61) + 1 = 192 + 62 + 1 = 255 octets. The total label-data content is 3*63 + 61 = 250 octets. In presentation form this is 63.63.63.61, which is 253 characters without the trailing dot and 254 with it. The 255 figure is wire octets, not characters.
- Maximum number of labels: 127 one-octet labels: 127*(1+1) + 1 = 255 octets.
- Root name: one zero octet, 1 octet.

## Clarifications

- The 255 count includes the terminating root label's zero octet. Excluding it would give 254, which is not the specification's count.
- Compression pointers are two-octet pointers. They may make a name's representation in a message shorter, but they do not change the logical name. The 255-octet limit applies to the uncompressed name.
- Presentation-format length can exceed 253 characters when escaping is required, for example when dots or non-printable octets are escaped. The octet limit is on the wire encoding, not on escaped text.
- Some APIs or later guidance use a 253-character presentation limit. That is a presentation or implementation convention, not a different RFC 1035 wire limit.
- The label limit and name limit are independent: a label may be at most 63 octets, and a full name may be at most 255 octets.

## Final values

Label: 63 octets of label data, or 64 octets including the length octet.

Full domain name: 255 octets in uncompressed wire encoding, including all label length octets and the root terminator.

This new rule will significantly reduce the level of PFAS in drinking water across the United States. Many states
have worked to monitor for and reduce PFAS exposure in drinking water through state-specific regulations. This
rule builds on these efforts by incorporating the latest science and establishing a nationwide, long-term health-
protective level for these specific PFAS in drinking water. Communities and states will need to determine
whether PFAS is in their drinking water and take actions such as notifying consumers and reducing the levels of
PFAS, as needed.
Water systems must take action to reduce the levels of these PFAS in drinking water if the level of PFAS in their
drinking water exceeds regulatory standards. Regulated public water systems have three years to complete their
initial monitoring for these chemicals. Systems must include their results in their Annual Water Quality reports
to customers. Systems that detect PFAS above the new standards will have five years to implement solutions
that reduce PFAS in their drinking water. Water systems must also notify the public if levels of regulated PFAS
exceed these new standards.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

US federal Maximum Contaminant Level (MCL) for PFOA in drinking water:

- As the rule lists it: 4.0 parts per trillion (ppt) — the rule text also writes it as "4.0 nanograms per liter (ng/L) or parts per trillion (ppt)".
- In nanograms per litre: 4.0 ng/L (identical to 4.0 ppt for water; conversion factor is exactly 1, so no rounding is applied and the rule's two significant figures are preserved).

AUTHORITY AND CITATION

- Rule: PFAS National Primary Drinking Water Regulation (PFAS NPDWR), final rule, 89 FR 32532 (page 32535 et seq.), published in the Federal Register on 26 April 2024 (FR Doc. 2024-07773), issued under the Safe Drinking Water Act.
- Verbatim from the rule's preamble/regulatory summary: "the EPA is promulgating individual Maximum Contaminant Levels (MCLs) for PFOA and PFOS at 4.0 nanograms per liter (ng/L) or parts per trillion (ppt)."
- Verbatim from EPA's summary table for the same rule: "PFOA — Final MCLG: Zero — Final MCL (enforceable levels): 4.0 parts per trillion (ppt) (also expressed as ng/L)."
- Codification: the MCLs are promulgated as amendments to the National Primary Drinking Water Regulations at 40 CFR part 141. Compliance is determined by running annual averages at the sampling point.

UNIT CONVERSION (shown, not assumed)

- 1 ppt = 1 part per 10^12 parts.
- For water, 1 L has a mass of about 1 kg = 10^12 ng (1 ng = 10^-9 g).
- Therefore 1 ppt ≈ 1 ng/L for aqueous samples, and 4.0 ppt = 4.0 ng/L exactly, with no arithmetic change and no rounding.
- The rule itself supplies this equivalence ("ng/L or ppt"), so the ng/L figure is the rule's own expression, not an outside conversion.

WHAT THIS VALUE IS AND IS NOT

- It is an enforceable MCL, applying to community and non-transient non-community public water systems.
- It is not the MCLG. The MCLG for PFOA is zero (0) — a non-enforceable health goal. The enforceable MCL of 4.0 ng/L is set as close to that goal as is feasible.
- It is not the Hazard Index MCL. That is a separate, unitless limit of 1 applying to mixtures of two or more of PFHxS, PFNA, HFPO-DA and PFBS. PFOA is expressly excluded from the Hazard Index (PFOA and PFOS are regulated individually as likely carcinogens).
- It is not a combined PFOA+PFOS limit; the rule sets separate individual MCLs of 4.0 ng/L for each of PFOA and PFOS.
- It is a federal value. States may set limits no less strict than the NPDWR; stricter state limits are outside this answer.

STATUS CAVEAT FOR THE READER

The MCL value of 4.0 ng/L is as promulgated in the 2024 final rule (effective 26 June 2024, with MCL compliance obligations beginning in 2029). Compliance-deadline extensions or implementation adjustments do not alter the promulgated MCL number, but because the rule has been subject to subsequent administrative and judicial activity, anyone relying on this for enforcement purposes should confirm current status against EPA's PFAS NPDWR page and the Federal Register docket (EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0114) at the time of use. Nothing in the sourced rule text supports any value other than 4.0 ng/L (4.0 ppt) for PFOA.

5.2.  The 425 (Too Early) Status Code
A 425 (Too Early) status code indicates that the server is unwilling
to risk processing a request that might be replayed.
User agents that send a request in early data are expected to retry
the request when receiving a 425 (Too Early) response status code.  A
user agent SHOULD retry automatically, but any retries MUST NOT be
sent in early data.
In all cases, an intermediary can forward a 425 (Too Early) status
code.  Intermediaries MUST forward a 425 (Too Early) status code if
the request that it received and forwarded contained an Early-Data
header field.  Otherwise, an intermediary that receives a request in
early data MAY automatically retry that request in response to a 425
(Too Early) status code, but it MUST wait for the TLS handshake to
complete on the connection where it received the request.
The server cannot assume that a client is able to retry a request
unless the request is received in early data or the Early-Data header
field is set to "1".  A server SHOULD NOT emit the 425 status code
unless one of these conditions is met.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

Status code 425 in the IANA "Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Status Code Registry":

  Value:        425
  Name:         Too Early
  Reference:    RFC 8470

So: (1) the name of 425 is **Too Early**; (2) its reference is **RFC 8470**.

EVIDENCE (registry row, verbatim from the IANA machine-readable CSV export)

The CSV at https://www.iana.org/assignments/http-status-codes/http-status-codes-1.csv (registry last updated 2025-09-15) contains the row:

  425,Too Early,[RFC 8470]

in the columns Value,Description,Reference. The neighbouring rows show that this is the correct reading of the row and that the citation carries no section number:

  424,Failed Dependency,[RFC 4918]
  425,Too Early,[RFC 8470]
  426,Upgrade Required,"[RFC 9110, Section 15.5.22]"

CROSS-CHECK 1 — HTML rendering (https://www.iana.org/assignments/http-status-codes)

The HTML table renders the same row as three cells: '425' / 'Too Early' / 'RFC 8470'.

CROSS-CHECK 2 — XML rendering (http-status-codes.xml)

The XML export lists 425 followed by 'Too Early', and 426 followed by 'Upgrade Required', matching the HTML/CSV ordering.

CROSS-CHECK 3 — the defining RFC's own registration (RFC 8470, Section 7, "IANA Considerations")

RFC 8470 ("Using Early Data in HTTP", M. Thomson, M. Lassey, C. Sethi; September 2018; Standards Track) states in Section 7:

  This document registers the 425 (Too Early) status code in the "HTTP
  Status Codes" registry located at <https://www.iana.org/assignments/
  http-status-codes>.

  Value:  425
  Description:  Too Early
  Reference:  This document

"This document" = RFC 8470, which confirms the registry's Reference field independently of the registry page itself. The code's semantics are defined in RFC 8470 Section 5.2, "The 425 (Too Early) Status Code": "A 425 (Too Early) status code indicates that the server is unwilling to risk processing a request that might be replayed." That section also specifies that a 425 is not cacheable by default and that intermediaries MUST forward it when the forwarded request carried an Early-Data header field.

CAVEATS / PRECISION NOTES

- The registry's own top-level Reference field is 'RFC 9110, Section 16.2.1: HTTP Semantics'. That is the reference for the registry as a whole, NOT the reference for 425. The per-row reference for 425 is RFC 8470. Do not substitute RFC 9110 for this answer.
- The registry field is named 'Description'; it is reported here as the status code's name, which is the standard usage. The registered description string is exactly 'Too Early' (capital T, capital E, no trailing punctuation, no parenthetical).
- RFC 8470 is not obsoleted and the 425 entry carries no errata or obsoletion annotation in the registry, so there is no reference chain to resolve: the single, primary, and only defining RFC is RFC 8470. (Contrast 510, which does carry a '; Status change of HTTP experiments to Historic' annotation.)
- Related registrations in the same RFC: RFC 8470 also registers the Early-Data header field in the 'Permanent Message Header Field Names' registry. This is context only and does not affect the two answers.

VERIFICATION (single check, since no falsifiers were requested)

Re-read the row '425,Too Early,[RFC 8470]' against both answers: name field = 'Too Early' = ask 1; reference field = 'RFC 8470' = ask 2. No other numeric value is asserted in this deliverable, so no self-imposed bound or threshold can be violated.

7.1 Overview
The LM317 is a 500-mA linear regulator with high voltage tolerance up to 40-V. The device has a feedback

superior line and load regulation. It also allows the LM317 to be used as a current source or current sink using a
single resistor. Any output voltage output voltage from 1.25-V to 37-V can be obtained by using two resistors.
