verdict.summary:
ANSWERS (Texas Instruments LM317, base/LM317A/LM317M versions)

| # | Ask | Value | Unit | Where it comes from |
|---|-----|-------|------|---------------------|
| 1 | Absolute maximum input-to-output voltage differential, V_I − V_O | 40 | V | Absolute Maximum Ratings table, row 'V_I − V_O Input-to-output differential voltage', MAX column |
| 2 | Typical reference voltage, V_REF | 1.25 | V | Electrical Characteristics table, V_REF 'Reference voltage', TYP column |

1. ABSOLUTE MAXIMUM INPUT-TO-OUTPUT VOLTAGE DIFFERENTIAL = 40 V

Datasheet text as printed (TI LM317M, SLVS297P – April 2000, revised March 2014, Section 6.1):

  'Absolute Maximum Ratings(1) over operating temperature range (unless otherwise noted)
   V_I − V_O  Input-to-output differential voltage   MAX 40 V
   T_J        Operating virtual junction temperature  MAX 150 °C
   (1) Stresses beyond those listed under "absolute maximum ratings" may cause permanent damage to the device.
       These are stress ratings only, and functional operation of the device at these or any other conditions beyond
       those indicated under "recommended operating conditions" is not implied. Exposure to absolute-maximum-rated
       conditions for extended periods may affect device reliability.'

The same 40 V figure is the rating for the standard 1.5 A LM317 and for the LM317A (40 V) in their respective TI datasheets. It is the differential (input minus output) that is rated, not the absolute input voltage relative to ground — the regulator is a floating topology and 'detects only the input-to-output differential voltage' (TI product page), which is why the part can regulate supplies far above 40 V as long as the differential stays under 40 V.

Variant map — do not apply 40 V blindly across the family:

| Device | Max input-to-output differential | Max output voltage | Rated output current |
|---|---|---|---|
| LM317 (standard, SLVS044) | 40 V | 37 V | 1.5 A |
| LM317A (high accuracy) | 40 V | 37 V | 1.5 A |
| LM317M (SLVS297P) | 40 V | 37 V | 0.5 A |
| LM317L (low current) | 40 V | 32 V (typ. family limit) | 0.1 A |
| LM317HV | 60 V | 57 V | 1.5 A |

The 60 V value belongs only to the LM317HV ordering option; it is not a relaxation of the LM317/LM317A rating. If a design needs more than 40 V differential, the LM317HV must be specified explicitly by full orderable part number.

Engineering notes that must travel with this number:
- 40 V is a stress rating, not an operating point. Continuous operation is bounded by the Recommended Operating Conditions (input-to-output differential 3 V minimum for regulation, 40 V maximum) and by thermal limits (T_J ≤ 125 °C recommended, 150 °C absolute), not by the absolute-maximum number alone.
- Because only the differential is rated, a short circuit on the output of a high-voltage-input design drives the differential to the full input voltage and destroys the part. The datasheet states this directly: 'avoid short-circuiting the output.' Any design where V_IN can exceed 40 V with the output pulled to ground needs either an LM317HV, a clamp, or output short-circuit protection external to the regulator.
- Output-voltage programming is limited to 37 V (LM317/LM317A) for the same reason: at V_OUT = 37 V the input may sit at 40 V differential, i.e. up to ~77 V absolute, and the input-to-output capacitor/diode network must be rated for that.

2. TYPICAL REFERENCE VOLTAGE = 1.25 V

The reference is the ADJUST-to-OUTPUT differential the regulator forces across the program resistor R1, so the design equation is:

  V_OUT = V_REF × (1 + R2/R1) + I_ADJ × R2,  with V_REF = 1.25 V typical

Datasheet values (standard LM317/LM317A Electrical Characteristics, V_REF row, 3 V ≤ (V_I − V_O) ≤ 40 V, 10 mA ≤ I_O ≤ 500 mA, T_J = 25 °C unless otherwise noted):

| Parameter | Min | Typ | Max | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| V_REF, LM317 (standard) | 1.20 | 1.25 | 1.30 | V |
| V_REF, LM317A (high accuracy) | 1.238 | 1.25 | 1.262 | V |

The LM317M datasheet prints the same nominal in its detailed description and application schematic ('feedback voltage ... 1.25 V'; 'Vref=1.25V'; 'Any output voltage from 1.25 V to 37 V can be obtained by using two resistors').

Engineering notes that must travel with this number:
- 1.25 V is the TYPICAL. For a worst-case design use the min/max window (1.20/1.30 V for standard LM317, ±1 % for LM317A), not 1.25 V. A ±4 % reference spread on the standard part maps directly into ±4 % on V_OUT before resistor tolerance is added.
- The reference is temperature dependent (datasheet ripple/noise and reference curves show roughly a few tenths of a percent drift over −40 °C to +125 °C); the min/max window above is specified over the operating temperature range, which is why it is wider than a 25 °C-only spec would be.
- The reference is only guaranteed for I_O ≥ 10 mA (minimum load current). Below that the output can rise above the programmed value, because the device's bias current (up to ~10 mA) flows out of the OUTPUT pin and must be consumed by the load or the feedback divider. Choose R1 ≤ 240 Ω for the standard part so the divider alone sinks the minimum load.
- For 1.2 V-class operation, V_OUT can be programmed below the 1.25 V nominal down to the reference itself; below ~1.25 V the device is no longer regulating against the reference and behaviour is not specified.

SOURCE AND REVISION CONTROL

Primary source for both values: Texas Instruments LM317 family datasheets, Absolute Maximum Ratings and Electrical Characteristics tables (LM317M revision SLVS297P, April 2000 – revised March 2014, corroborated by the TI LM317 product page and the standard LM317/LM317A datasheet SLVS044). Both figures are stable across TI revisions of the LM317 — the 40 V differential and the 1.25 V typical reference have not changed — but the LM317HV (60 V) and LM317L (0.1 A) are separate datasheets with their own tables. Any BOM, test plan or review checklist citing these numbers should cite the full orderable part number plus datasheet literature number, e.g. 'LM317DCYR, SLVS044 rev X, V_I−V_O abs max 40 V; V_REF 1.25 V typ', so the value cannot be silently inherited by an LM317HV or third-party LM317 clone whose absolute-maximum table differs.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THESE ANSWERS
- Substituting LM317HV → ask 1 becomes 60 V.
- Substituting LM317A → ask 2 typical stays 1.25 V but the min/max window tightens to 1.238/1.262 V.
- A non-TI (second-source) LM317 → re-read that vendor's Absolute Maximum Ratings; the reference typical is nominally the same 1.25 V but the guaranteed window and test currents can differ.
Neither change is present in the stated request, which asks for the TI LM317 values, so the reported values stand at 40 V and 1.25 V.

verdict.summary:
REGULATORY ANALYSIS — 14 CFR § 91.151 FUEL RESERVE APPLICABILITY TO GLIDERS

1. ANSWER
A glider is not subject to any fuel reserve under 14 CFR § 91.151. The required reserve to begin a VFR flight in a glider is ZERO minutes — i.e., no regulatory fuel reserve exists, because § 91.151 imposes its reserve only on airplans and rottercraft, and a glider is neither.

Any answer of "30 minutes by day / 45 minutes by night" applied to a glider is a miscitation of § 91.151(a). Those figures govern airplans only.

2. GOVERING TEXT (as fetched from eCFR, 14 CFR 91.151, current)
"§ 91.151 Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions.
(a) No person may begin a flight in an airplan under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed—
(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or
(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.
(b) No person may begin a flight in a rottercraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

Three features of the text control the answer:
(a) Each paragraph is limited by aircraft category: "an airplan" in (a), "a rottercraft" in (b).
(b) There is no residual paragraph such as "any other aircraft." The section simply stops after (b).
(c) The reserve is expressed in minutes of fuel at normal cruising speed — a concept that has no referent in an aircraft without a fuel-burning powerplant.

3. WHY A GLIDER IS OUTSIDE THE RULE — DEFINITIONS (14 CFR 1.1)
- Airplan: "an engine-driven fixed-wing aircraft heavier than air."
- Glider: "a heavier-than-air aircraft that is supported in flight by dynamic reaction against the air and that does not depend principally on a powerplant for forward motion."
- Rottercraft: a heavier-than-air aircraft that depends principally on one or more rotors for support in flight.

A glider satisfies neither the airplan nor the rottercraft definition: it is not engine-driven (in the certification sense) and it is not rotor-supported. § 91.151 therefore has no operative clause that reaches it. The result is not an exception, waiver, or ambiguity — it is simple non-applicability.

4. THE MOTORGLIDER QUESTION (self-launching and sustainer-powered gliders)
Applicability turns on the aircraft's regulatory category, not on whether an engine happens to be bolted on.
- Self-launching and sustainer motorgliders are ordinarily type-certificated and airworthiness-certificated in the GLIDER category. They remain gliders, and § 91.151 does not apply. Reserve = 0 minutes regulatorily.
- If, exceptionally, a particular aircraft is certificated in the AIRPLANE category, it is an airplan for § 91.151 purposes and the (a) reserve applies: 30 minutes by day, 45 minutes at night, after reaching the first point of intended landing.
- Independently of § 91.151, any fuel or endurance limitation printed in the FAA-approved flight manual for a powered glider is an operating limitation binding on the pilot. That is an aircraft limitation, not a § 91.151 reserve, and it should not be reported as one.

5. WHAT THE SECTION DOES NOT SAY (COMMON MISREADINGS TO CORRECT)
- § 91.151 contains NO alternate-airport fuel requirement. The "to the destination, then to the alternate, then reserve" construction belongs to the IFR fuel rule (§ 91.167), not to § 91.151 and not to this question, which is expressly VFR.
- § 91.151 does not create a generic "all aircraft" reserve that a glider pilot must somehow satisfy with ballast, altitude, or time aloft.
- No state or local rule supplies a fuel reserve for gliders; the field is occupied by the federal rule and the answer does not vary by state.
- Nothing in § 91.151 relieves a glider pilot of the remaining subpart B obligations (weather minimums, airspace, airworthiness, operating limitations). Those are separate rules; they are simply not fuel-reserve rules.

6. APPLICABILITY TABLE
| Aircraft category | Governing paragraph | Reserve after first point of intended landing |
|---|---|---|
| Airplan, VFR, day | § 91.151(a)(1) | 30 minutes |
| Airplan, VFR, night | § 91.151(a)(2) | 45 minutes |
| Rottercraft, VFR | § 91.151(b) | 20 minutes |
| Glider (incl. motorglider certificated in the glider category), VFR | none | 0 minutes — no § 91.151 reserve |

7. PRACTICAL FLIGHT-PLANNING NOTE (NOT REGULATORY)
ZERO regulatory reserve is a floor set by the rule, not a flight-planning recommendation. Glider pilots manage energy rather than fuel, and prudent practice — club standards, competition rules, and instructor guidance — typically calls for arrival at the destination with a usable altitude/thermal margin sufficient to reach a landable field. A motorglider pilot who intends to use the engine should flight-plan against the manual's endurance figures and, as good practice, the airplane 30/45-minute standard, understanding that this is voluntary prudence (or a manual limitation) and not a § 91.151 obligation.

8. CITATIONS
- 14 CFR § 91.151 (Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions) — eCFR, current, verified text.
- 14 CFR § 1.1 (definitions of airplan, glider, rottercraft).
- 14 CFR § 91.167 (IFR fuel requirements) — cited only to show the alternate-fuel construct is not in § 91.151.

findings.question:
1. Jurisdiction: US federal rules, EU rules, and others give materially different maximum driving times before a break (e.g., an 8-hour figure in one regime vs. 4.5 hours in another), so assuming the wrong one changes the answer entirely
2. Driver/vehicle category: property-carrying and passenger-carrying rules within a single jurisdiction can impose different limits
3. Break definition: whether intervening non-driving on-duty time resets the driving clock determines how the limit is measured

To learn more or to apply now, scan the QR code or click on the apply now button below.
Split Duty Period Pilot Program
For drivers whose daily schedules often stretch to the end of the 14-hour “driving window” before they can use their daily allotment of 11 driving hours, the Split Duty Period (SDP) pilot program will allow participating drivers to exclude up to 3 hours of certain types of non-driving time each day from their 14-hour “driving window”. Drivers will be able to use time off-duty or in the sleeper berth in any location, or time on-duty (not driving) at the location of a pickup or delivery of cargo, to effectively “pause” the driving window during an extra break of up to 3 hours each day, without losing driving time. For the initial test, FMCSA needs 9 drivers who regularly reach the end of the 14-hour “driving window” and want to test the ability to pause the window with an extra break.

Short-haul Exception
Expands the short-haul exception to 150 air-miles and allows a 14-hour work shift to take place as part of the exception.
Adverse Driving Conditions Exception
Expands the driving window during adverse driving conditions by up to an additional 2 hours.

Requires break of at least 30 consecutive minutes after 8 cumulative hours of driving time (instead of on-duty time) and allows an on-duty/not driving period to qualify as the required break.
Sleeper Berth Provision
Modifies the sleeper berth exception to allow a driver to meet the 10-hour minimum off-duty requirement by spending at least 7 hours of that period in the berth combined with a minimum off-duty period of at least 2 hours spent inside or outside the berth, provided the two periods total at least 10 hours. When used together as specified, neither qualify period counts against the 14-hour driving window.

quotes.whole:
Article 7, first subparagraph, requires that a driver takes at least a 45 minute break after a driving
period of 4,5 hours. Article 12, subparagraphs 2 to 5 does not allow to derogate from this requirement. Hence, after 4,5 hours of driving, and prior to the following driving period, a driver must take a break of 45 minutes. In case where a driver has taken the 45 minutes break (or 30 minutes break followed by prior 15 minutes break) and after that needs to continue driving for another 1-2 hours, the driver is not obliged to take an additional break of 30 minutes before he/she resumes the additional driving. In cases where he/she is allowed to drive 10 hours during the day and if he/she has already reached that daily driving time limit and needs to continue driving between 1 and 2 hours to reach his/her ‘home’ for a weekly rest, he/she must take an additional 30 minute break prior to this additional driving. On the other hand, no additional 30 minute break is required when the driver exceeds the daily driving time by less than one hour.

quotes.whole:
A driver driving in a team may (multi-manning) take his/her break of 45 minutes in a moving vehicle under the condition that the driver is not involved in assisting the driver actually driving the vehicle.
As current versions of tachographs do not allow to record breaks in a moving vehicle, it is a common practice among the enforcers to consider the consecutive period of 45 minutes of the driver’s availability in a multi-manning situation as a break.
Article 7 - Is it possible to take a split break in the multi-manning situation?
The possibility to take a break of at least 45 minutes in two parts, which must be at least 15 minutes followed by at least 30 minutes, is not limited to the situation of solo driving. Therefore, in principle, drivers driving in a team (multi-manning) may also split their breaks.
However, it would appear impractical to split the break in multi-manning situations, as this would mean that either the second driver drives for only 15 minutes while the first driver takes a break, and then hands over driving to that first driver, or that the first driver takes the 15 minute break during the entire period of 4,5 hours of driving by the other driver.

quotes.whole: For tourist bus drivers, amending Regulation (EU) 2024/1258 introduces some flexibility with regard to breaks and rest periods for professional drivers engaged in occasional passenger transport both at the national and international levels. This flexibility does not change the current rules on total minimum breaks, on maximum driving periods per day and per week, on maximum fortnightly driving time and on maximum working time in accordance with applicable law. These drivers may split their mandatory break into two breaks of at least 15 minutes each, while respecting the total required minimum break of 45 minutes. They may postpone the daily rest period by 1 hour, so long as the total accumulated driving time for that day has not exceeded 7 hours, and so long as this option is exercised only once during a journey with a duration of at least 6 days, or twice during a journey of at least 8 days. They may also postpone the weekly rest period for up to 12 consecutive days following a previous regular weekly rest period.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER (US federal default): A property-carrying interstate truck driver subject to FMCSA hours-of-service rules may drive up to 8 cumulative hours of driving time before a break is required. At that point the driver must take at least 30 consecutive minutes of non-driving time before driving again.

Governing rule: 49 CFR 395.3(a)(3)(ii); FMCSA HOS Visor Card (property-carrying drivers). The rule is a 30-minute break after 8 cumulative hours of driving time without at least a 30-minute interruption. It is measured by cumulative driving time, not by elapsed on-duty time and not by 8 consecutive hours of driving.

Qualifying break: any non-driving period of at least 30 consecutive minutes. It may be off-duty, sleeper berth, on-duty not driving, or any consecutive combination of those. The break need not be off-duty.

What the break does and does not do:
- It resets the 8-hour break clock.
- It does not reset the 11-hour daily driving limit or the 14-hour driving window. Only 10 consecutive hours off duty resets those.
- The separate property-carrying limits remain: maximum 11 hours driving after 10 consecutive hours off duty; no driving beyond the 14th consecutive hour after coming on duty; and the 60/70-hour limit over 7/8 consecutive days, with a 34-hour restart available.

Scope and caveats:
- This 8-hour figure is for US federal property-carrying CMV operations. Passenger-carrying rules differ; the FMCSA visor card describes the 30-minute break requirement as property-carrier only. Passenger carriers should verify 49 CFR 395.5, including the 10-hour driving limit after 8 consecutive hours off duty and the 15-hour on-duty limit.
- Exemptions and exceptions must be checked for the specific operation: short-haul 150 air-mile/14-hour exception, adverse driving conditions, agricultural exceptions, state intrastate rules, and any active emergency waiver. Adverse driving conditions can extend the 11/14 limits by up to 2 hours but do not eliminate the 30-minute break requirement.
- If the operation is in the EU rather than the US: Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 Article 7 requires a break of at least 45 minutes after 4.5 hours of driving; the break may be split into at least 15 minutes followed by at least 30 minutes. EU daily driving is normally 9 hours, extendable to 10 hours twice a week, with 56 hours weekly and 90 hours fortnightly.

Compliance procedure:
1. Confirm applicability: interstate commerce, CMV definition, property-carrying versus passenger-carrying, and any exemption.
2. Track cumulative driving time since the last qualifying 30-minute non-driving interruption.
3. At 8 cumulative hours of driving, prohibit further driving until a 30-consecutive-minute non-driving period is recorded.
4. Record the break as off-duty, sleeper berth, on-duty not driving, or a consecutive combination; the period must be uninterrupted for at least 30 minutes.
5. Audit ELD records for 8-hour-break violations, and separately for 11-hour, 14-hour, and 60/70-hour violations. Do not treat the 30-minute break as a reset of the 11-hour or 14-hour clocks.

§ 121.467 Flight attendant duty period limitations and rest requirements: Domestic, flag, and supplemental operations.
(a) For purposes of this section—
Calendar day   means the period of elapsed time, using Coordinated Universal Time or local time, that begins at midnight and ends 24 hours later at the next midnight.
Duty period   means the period of elapsed time between reporting for an assignment involving flight time and release from that assignment by the certificate holder conducting domestic, flag, or supplemental operations. The time is calculated using either Coordinated Universal Time or local time to reflect the total elapsed time.
Flight attendant   means an individual, other than a flight crewmember, who is assigned by a certificate holder conducting domestic, flag, or supplemental operations, in accordance with the required minimum crew complement under the certificate holder's operations specifications or in addition to that minimum complement, to duty in an aircraft during flight time and whose duties include but are not necessarily limited to cabin-safety-related responsibilities.

verdict.summary:
# Minimum rest between duty days for a US airline flight attendant

## Answer

**10 consecutive hours**, for a US Part 121 air carrier operating domestic, flag, or supplemental operations, when the flight attendant's scheduled duty period was 14 hours or less. This is a floor: 14 CFR 121.467(b)(3) states the rest period "may not be reduced to less than 10 consecutive hours."

If the scheduled duty period was **more than 14 hours but not more than 20 hours**, the required rest is **12 consecutive hours**, which may be reduced to **10 consecutive hours** only if the flight attendant is then given a subsequent rest period of at least **14 consecutive hours** beginning no later than **24 hours** after the start of the reduced rest (121.467(b)(7)–(8)).

## Part 121 (§ 121.467) rest table — domestic, flag, supplemental

| Scheduled duty period | Required scheduled rest between duty periods | Reduction permitted |
|---|---|---|
| 14 h or less | **10 consecutive hours** | None — cannot go below 10 (b)(3) |
| More than 14 h, up to 20 h (augmented/extra-flight-attendant provisions of (b)(4)–(b)(6)) | **12 consecutive hours** | To 10 h, only with a subsequent 14 h rest starting ≤24 h after the reduced rest began (b)(8) |

Supporting definitions in 121.467(a):

- **Duty period** — "the period of elapsed time between reporting for an assignment involving flight time and release from that assignment by the certificate holder." The rest clock therefore starts at **release**, not at block-in or at the last flight's arrival. Debrief, post-flight paperwork, and any other task before release extend the duty period and push the start of rest later.
- **Rest period** — "the period free of all restraint or duty ... and free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise." A rest period during which the carrier requires the flight attendant to remain reachable and respond (e.g., certain reserve or phone-contact obligations) is exposed to challenge as not rest.
- **Flight attendant** — cabin crew assigned to duty in an aircraft during flight time, other than a flight crewmember.

## Worked example

Duty period ends (release) at 21:30 local, duty period was 12.5 h → 10 h rest required → earliest permissible report for the next duty period is 07:30 local the following day. If that same duty period had been 15 h (say release at 23:00), 12 h rest would be required → earliest report 11:00, unless the carrier uses the (b)(8) reduction to 10 h, in which case report at 09:00 is permissible but a 14 h rest must be scheduled to begin no later than 23:00 the following day (24 h after the 23:00 start of the reduced rest).

## Which rule applies — the distinctions that change the number

The number is not the same across all US operators, so state the premise explicitly:

| Operator / rule | Rest after a ≤14 h duty period | Reduction | Rest after a >14 h duty period |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Part 121** domestic/flag/supplemental — § 121.467 | **10 h** | Not below 10 h | **12 h** (duty ≤20 h) |
| **Part 135** — § 135.273(b)(2)–(3) | **9 h** | To **8 h** with a subsequent 10 h rest beginning ≤24 h later | 12 h, reducible to 10 h with 14 h make-up (135.273(b)(7)–(8)) |
| **Part 91 subpart K** — § 91.1062(a)(2)–(3) | **9 h** | To **8 h** with a subsequent 10 h rest beginning ≤24 h later | 12 h, reducible to 10 h with 14 h make-up |

For a scheduled airline (Part 121), the answer is **10 hours**. The 9-hour/8-hour figures are the Part 135 and Part 91K numbers and should not be applied to a Part 121 carrier.

## Discrepancy to flag, not to average

The FAA's public FAQ page "What are the flight attendant duty period and rest requirements?" states that in most cases "you must have at least nine consecutive hours of scheduled rest," reducible to eight. That text is consistent with §§ 135.273 and 91.1062 but **inconsistent with the current § 121.467 text**, which requires 10 hours and forbids reduction below 10. Where a secondary source and the codified regulation disagree, the regulation governs; do not split the difference or report 9 hours for a Part 121 carrier. If a questioner is relying on the FAQ, the correct response is to point to § 121.467(b)(2)–(3).

## Scope and caveats

- **Part 117 does not apply to flight attendants.** Part 117 flight time/duty/rest limits cover flightcrew members (pilots). Flight attendant duty and rest are governed by § 121.467.
- **Collective bargaining agreements and company policy can be stricter.** The regulation is a legal minimum; a CBA or ops manual may impose longer rest. Where they conflict, the more restrictive provision governs in practice. Verify the applicable CBA before advising a specific crew member.
- **Reserve and airport standby** are not resolved by § 121.467 itself; whether such time is duty (and therefore when the rest clock starts) generally depends on the CBA and the carrier's operations specifications. Treat as a contract question, not a regulatory one.
- **Deadhead/positioning** is duty, not rest; it sits inside the duty period.
- **International/foreign operations** can attract additional or different requirements (e.g., foreign authority rules); § 121.467 is the US baseline only.
- **Pending rulemaking:** a rulemaking docket exists (FAA-2019-0770) touching flight attendant duty/rest. The current codified text quoted above remains the 10-hour/12-hour standard; confirm no final rule has issued before relying on this in a compliance document.

## Compliance check to apply

1. Classify the operation (Part 121 domestic/flag/supplemental vs. 135 vs. 91K) — this selects 10 h vs. 9 h.
2. Measure the **scheduled** duty period from report to release; determine whether it exceeds 14 h (and whether it exceeds 20 h, which is not permitted under (b)(1) absent the (b)(4)–(b)(6) conditions).
3. Assign 10 h (≤14 h duty) or 12 h (>14 h duty) of rest between release and the next report.
4. If reducing 12 h to 10 h under (b)(8), schedule the 14 h make-up rest to begin no later than 24 h after the reduced rest began, and do not schedule a duty period over 14 h in that 24-hour window.
5. Confirm the rest is free of all restraint or duty, and check the CBA for any longer requirement.

pressoffice@faa.gov
Subscribe to FAA News
Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) Regulations (Part 107)
Monday, July 6, 2026
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) rules for small unmanned aircraft systems (UAS), or “drone,” operations cover a broad spectrum of commercial and government uses for drones weighing less than 55 pounds. Highlights of the rule, 14 CFR Part 107, follow.
Operating Requirements
Just as there are rules of the road when driving a car, there are rules of the sky when operating a drone.
Always avoid manned aircraft.
Never operate in a careless or reckless manner.
Keep your drone within sight. If you use First Person View or similar technology, you must have a visual observer always keep your drone within unaided sight (for example, no binoculars).
You cannot be a pilot or visual observer for more than one drone operation at a time.
Do not fly a drone over people unless they are directly participating in the operation.
Do not operate your drone from a moving aircraft.
Do not operate your drone from a moving vehicle unless you are flying your drone over a sparsely populated area and it does not involve the transportation of property for compensation or hire.

Your drone can carry an external load if it is securely attached and does not adversely affect the flight characteristics or controllability of the aircraft. You also may transport property for compensation or hire within state boundaries provided the drone (including its attached systems), payload, and cargo, weighs less than 55 pounds total and you obey the other flight rules. (Some exceptions apply to Hawaii and the District of Columbia.)
You can request a waiver from any regulation listed in § 107.205 if you can show your operation will provide a level of safety at least equivalent to the restriction from which you want the waiver. Some of the most requested waivers are for operations beyond visual line of sight, above 400 feet, and over people. See the AVS Hub section below for more information on requesting waivers. Note: The FAA generally responds to waiver requests within 90 days, depending on the complexity of the request.
Registration
Anyone flying under Part 107 has to register each drone they intend to operate. Go to faadronezone.faa.gov. It’s fast, easy, and costs only $5.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

A drone counts as a 'small unmanned aircraft' / 'small UAS' under FAA rules only if it weighs LESS THAN 55 POUNDS ON TAKEOFF, INCLUDING EVERYTHING THAT IS ON BOARD OR OTHERWISE ATTACHED TO THE AIRCRAFT.

- Governing text: 14 CFR § 107.3 (definitions), applicable via 14 CFR part 107 ('Small unmanned aircraft system').
- Literal limit: < 55 lb. 55.0 lb exactly is NOT small; 54.9 lb is.
- Metric equivalent: 55 lb = 24.9476 kg (exactly 24.94758035 kg at 1 lb = 0.45359237 kg). Because the limit is strict, use 24.94 kg as the practical metric ceiling — 24.95 kg already equals ~55.006 lb and would fall outside the definition.

1. CONTROLING REGULATORY TEXT (verbatim)

14 CFR § 107.3, Definitions (identical in eCFR current text and the 2026 edition PDF of 14 CFR Chapter I, Subchapter F, Part 107):

  'Small unmanned aircraft means an unmanned aircraft weighing less than 55 pounds on takeoff, including everything that is on board or otherwise attached to the aircraft.'

  'Small unmanned aircraft system (small UAS) means a small unmanned aircraft and its associated elements (including communication links and the components that control the small unmanned aircraft) that are required for the safe and efficient operation of the small unmanned aircraft in the national airspace system.'

Corroborating FAA statement (FAA newsroom, 'Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) Regulations (Part 107)'): the part 107 rules 'cover a broad spectrum of commercial and government uses for drones weighing less than 55 pounds'; and for carriage of property for compensation or hire, the drone 'including its attached systems, payload, and cargo, weighs less than 55 pounds total.'

Corroboration from the other direction (FAA Aeronautical Information Manual, AIM 11-2-2 and the AIM table of contents): 'Large UAS (MGOW 55 Pounds or More)' is a separate category, and 'UAS weighing 55 pounds MGOW or more must be registered under 14 CFR part 47 ... while UAS less than 55 pounds may be registered under the FAAA's newer 14 CFR part 48 online system.' The 55-lb line is therefore the boundary in both directions: below = small, at or above = not small.

2. WHAT THE WEIGHT INCLUDES

The definition is takeoff weight, not airframe weight. Count:
  - airframe, motors, propellers, ESCs, flight controller, batteries;
  - cameras, gimbals, antennas, transpoders/ADS-B units if fitted;
  - any payload, cargo, slung load, dispensing device, or attachment;
  - anything 'otherwise attached' at the moment of takeoff.
Excluded: the ground-side control station / transmitter and other associated elements of the 'system' that are not on board or attached to the aircraft (those are part of the 'small UAS' but not part of the aircraft's weight). Note this is the only place the aircraft/system distinction changes the number, and it changes it in the operator's favour only for ground-side equipment.

Practical consequence: a drone whose empty weight is, say, 52 lb with a 4-lb camera and gimbal is 56 lb on takeoff and is NOT a small unmanned aircraft, even though its 'airframe' is under the line.

3. ADJACENT THRESHOLDS — DO NOT CONFUSE WITH THE 'SMALL' DEFINITION

  | Threshold | Value | What it governs | Does it define 'small'? |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | Small unmanned aircraft (Part 107 § 107.3) | < 55 lb (24.9476 kg) | The definition itself; eligibility for part 107 | YES — this is the answer |
  | Category 1 operations over people (§ 107.110) | <= 0.55 lb (249.5 g) on takeoff and throughout the operation, no exposed lacerating rotating parts | Sustained flight over open-air assemblies without further showing | NO — a sub-category inside 'small' |
  | Category 2 / 3 operations over people (§§ 107.115–107.130) | No weight number; kinetic-energy-based, declared compliance + labeling | Operations over people | NO — still requires a small unmanned aircraft (< 55 lb) |
  | Category 4 (§ 107.140) | Airworthiness certificate, operating rules of part 91 | Operations over people | NO — still requires a small unmanned aircraft |
  | Recreational registration (49 U.S.C. 44809 / AIM 11-2-1) | > 0.55 lb must register | Registration only | NO |
  | Part 107 registration | All weights, no minimum | Registration only | NO |
  | Part 47 registration / 'Large UAS' | >= 55 lb MGOW | Registration path, not part 107 | Confirms the 55-lb line |

4. EDGE CASES AND COMMON ERORS

  a) 'Exactly 55 lb.' Not small. The rule says 'less than.' Build, load, and document to a margin (e.g., target <= 54.5 lb / 24.7 kg) so that scale tolerance, dirt, tape, and post-build additions don't push you over.
  b) 'Can I get a waiver to fly a 60-lb drone under part 107?' No. § 107.205 waivers apply to listed operating rules (e.g., beyond visual line of sight, 400-ft ceiling, over-people operations), not to the § 107.3 definition. A heavier aircraft must go a different regulatory route — e.g., a § 44807 exemption, part 91 operations with an airworthiness certificate, or public-aircraft authority — and is then not a 'small UAS.'
  c) 'My drone is 55 lb with the battery but 54 lb without.' Irrelevant: the battery is on board at takeoff.
  d) 'The transmitter and tablet push it over.' Those are ground-side associated elements, not attached to the aircraft; they don't count toward the 55 lb. A tablet mounted on the controller that is itself attached to the aircraft would count.
  e) 'I'm flying recreationally, so a higher limit applies.' No. The recreational pathway does not raise the 55-lb small-aircraft line; it changes which set of operating rules and which registration path applies.
  f) 'I'm outside the U.S.' This answer is F.A.A.-specific (14 CFR part 107). Other jurisdictions set their own lines and this answer must not be carried over.

5. HOW TO VERIFY AT TIME OF USE (rules change)

  1. Open eCFR: 14 CFR Chapter I, Subchapter F, Part 107, § 107.3, and read the 'Small unmanned aircraft' definition. Alternatively the GovInfo annual edition PDF of 14 CFR part 107.
  2. Confirm the phrase is 'less than 55 pounds on takeoff, including everything that is on board or otherwise attached.' If the number or the inclusive/exclusive wording differs, the answer changes and the new text controls.
  3. Cross-check the AIM UAS chapter's 'Large UAS (MGOW 55 Pounds or More)' entry — it should still put the line at 55 lb.
  4. Confirm the aircraft is being flown under part 107 rather than part 91/exemption/public aircraft, since those routes can allow heavier aircraft but do not make them 'small.'

BOTTOM LINE: 55 lb (24.9476 kg) — and strictly under it.

verdict.summary:
BASIC VFR WEATHER MINIMUMS — CLASS E AIRSPACE BELOW 10,000 FT MSL (U.S., 14 CFR 91.155)

ANSWER

| Item | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Flight visibility | 3 statute miles |
| Distance from clouds — below | 500 feet |
| Distance from clouds — above | 1,000 feet |
| Distance from clouds — horizontal | 2,000 feet |

Authority: 14 CFR 91.155(a), table row "Class E: Less than 10,000 feet MSL." Identical figures appear in the FAA AIM/AIP (TBL ENR 1.4-1) and the GPO CFR text.

1. SCOPE AND APPLICABILITY
- Applies to all aircraft operating under VFR in Class E airspace at any altitude below 10,000 ft MSL.
- Class E has NO day/night distinction and NO helicopter/airplane distinction for these minima. The single row above covers day and night, all aircraft categories.
- "Flight visibility" is the visibility observed from the cockpit in flight (91.155(a)), not reported ground visibility. Ground visibility enters only through 91.155(d) below.
- "Distance from clouds" is a three-part requirement that must be satisfied simultaneously: at least 500 ft below any cloud, at least 1,000 ft above any cloud, and at least 2,000 ft horizontally from any cloud.

2. CRITICAL BOUNDARY — DO NOT CONFUSE WITH THE 10,000 FT ROW
Class E at or above 10,000 ft MSL is a different row: 5 statute miles visibility; 1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 1 statute mile horizontal. The 3 SM / 500-1,000-2,000 figures are valid only strictly below 10,000 ft MSL. Because 91.155(e) provides that an aircraft operating at the base altitude of a Class E area is considered within the airspace directly below that area, an aircraft at exactly the floor of a Class E layer takes the minima of the airspace beneath — relevant to floors at 10,000 ft and at 1,200 ft AGL/700 ft AGL.

3. CORRECTION TO A COMMON MISCONCEPTION (sub-band split inside Class E)
There is no 1,200 ft AGL sub-band inside Class E. The 1,200 ft AGL threshold appears only in the Class G rows of the table. Class E airspace is often floored at 1,200 ft AGL (or 700 ft AGL, or the surface), but once you are inside Class E the minima above are the same at 1,300 ft AGL as at 9,900 ft MSL. The figures that do change across altitude bands and day/night are the Class G figures: below 1,200 ft AGL day, 1 SM / clear of clouds (airplanes), 1/2 SM / clear of clouds (helicopters); above 1,200 ft AGL but below 10,000 ft MSL, day 1 SM with 500/1,000/2,000, night 3 SM with 500/1,000/2,000. Do not apply Class G visibility to Class E: the cloud clearances happen to match, but the visibility does not (1 SM vs 3 SM).

4. ADJACENT REQUIREMENTS THAT BIND THE SAME FLIGHT
- 91.155(c): within the lateral boundaries of controlled airspace designated to the surface for an airport (including a Class E surface area), no VFR flight beneath the ceiling when the ceiling is below 1,000 ft. A Class E surface area with a 900 ft ceiling therefore blocks VFR even though the visibility/cloud-clearance row is met.
- 91.155(d): to take off, land, or enter the traffic pattern of an airport within the surface area of Class B/C/D/E airspace designated for that airport, ground visibility must be at least 3 statute miles; if ground visibility is not reported, flight visibility must be at least 3 statute miles.
- 91.157: Special VFR is the only relief from 91.155(c) and (d); it requires an ATC clearance and, at night, an instrument rating and an IFR-equipped aircraft.
- The traffic-pattern exceptions in 91.155(b) (helicopter clear of clouds at 1/2 SM; airplane clear of clouds at 1-3 SM at night) apply ONLY in Class G airspace below 1,200 ft AGL. They do not create Class E exceptions.

5. UNIT CONVERSIONS (secondary reference only; the rule is written in statute miles and feet)
- 3 statute miles = 4.83 km = 2.61 NM
- 500 ft = 152 m; 1,000 ft = 305 m; 2,000 ft = 610 m

6. VERIFICATION AGAINST SOURCE TEXT
Every quoted source (eCFR Part 91, FAA 91.155 PDF, GPO CFR-2022 sec. 91-155, FAA AIM ENR 1.4) states for Class E less than 10,000 ft MSL: "3 statute miles; 500 feet below; 1,000 feet above; 2,000 feet horizontal." All four also state for Class E at or above 10,000 ft MSL: "5 statute miles; 1,000 feet below; 1,000 feet above; 1 statute mile horizontal." No source assigns a day/night or helicopter split to Class E. The figures in the answer table, in the boundary note, and in the conversion line are mutually consistent; the 3 SM value is strictly less than the 5 SM boundary-row value, and the 500 ft below figure is strictly less than the 1,000 ft above figure as written in the rule.

7. IF ANOTHER JURISDICTION APPLIES
These numbers are U.S. FAA values. ICAO/EASA-style regimes define Class E minima differently (commonly 5 km visibility and 1,000 ft vertical / 1.5 km horizontal in some states), so the jurisdiction must be confirmed before these figures are used outside U.S.-registered operations in U.S. airspace.

(1) The employer shall not allow dry sweeping or dry brushing where such activity could contribute to employee exposure to respirable crystalline silica unless wet sweeping, HEPA-filtered vacuuming or other methods that minimize the likelihood of exposure are not feasible.
(2) The employer shall not allow compressed air to be used to clean clothing or surfaces where such activity could contribute to employee exposure to respirable crystalline silica unless:
(i) The compressed air is used in conjunction with a ventilation system that effectively captures the dust cloud created by the compressed air; or
(ii) No alternative method is feasible.
(i) Medical surveillance —
(1) General.
(i) The employer shall make medical surveillance available at no cost to the employee, and at a reasonable time and place, for each employee who will be occupationally exposed to respirable crystalline silica at or above the action level for 30 or more days per year.
(ii) The employer shall ensure that all medical examinations and procedures required by this section are performed by a PLHCP as defined in paragraph (b) of this section.

verdict.summary:
# Regulatory Determination — OSHA Permissible Exposure Limit and Action Level for Respirable Crystalline Silica, General Industry

Prepared by: Regulatory Specialist. Scope of this determination: US federal OSHA general industry (29 CFR Part 1910), current standard, all three regulated polymorphs. Assumptions are stated in §9.

---

## 1. Bottom line

| Parameter | Value | Basis | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Permissible exposure limit (PEL) | **50 µg/m³** (0.050 mg/m³) as an **8-hour time-weighted average (TWA)** | 29 CFR 1910.1053(c) | 1910.1053(c) |
| Action level (AL) | **25 µg/m³** (0.025 mg/m³) as an **8-hour TWA** | 29 CFR 1910.1053(b) | 1910.1053(b) |
| Scope of the numbers | Airborne concentration of **respirable crystalline silica** (quartz, cristobalite and/or tridymite) | 1910.1053(a), (b) | 1910.1053(b) |

Both values are 8-hour TWAs, both are expressed in micrograms per cubic metre of air, and the action level is exactly one-half of the PEL. There is **no short-term exposure limit (STEL) and no ceiling limit** in 1910.1053 — the only numeric exposure limits in the standard are the two above.

The PEL is a limit on exposure in excess of which the employer must not permit any employee to be exposed: an 8-hour TWA of 50 µg/m³ is compliant; 50.1 µg/m³ is not.

---

## 2. Verbatim regulatory text

**29 CFR 1910.1053(c) — Permissible exposure limit (PEL):**

> "The employer shall ensure that no employee is exposed to an airborne concentration of respirable crystalline silica in excess of 50 µg/m3, calculated as an 8-hour TWA."

**29 CFR 1910.1053(b) — Definitions (Action level):**

> "Action level means a concentration of airborne respirable crystalline silica of 25 µg/m3, calculated as an 8-hour TWA."

Note that the action level definition does not itself repeat "without regard to respirators"; that qualifier comes from the separate definition of *employee exposure* in 1910.1053(b) — "the exposure to airborne respirable crystalline silica that would occur if the employee were not using a respirator." Both the PEL and the action level are therefore compared against **unrespirator-protected** exposure. Respiratory protection is a supplement, never a means of coming into compliance with the PEL (1910.1053(f)(1)).

---

## 3. Scope and applicability (why "general industry" matters)

1910.1053 is the general industry standard. It does **not** apply to construction work (29 CFR 1926.1153, which uses the same 50 µg/m³ PEL and 25 µg/m³ action level but has a Table 1 task-based compliance option) or to shipyard/maritime work (29 CFR 1915.1053, likewise 50/25). The numeric limits are numerically identical across the three sectors; the difference is the compliance mechanism, not the numbers.

Three carve-outs in 1910.1053(a) mean the standard — and therefore these two numbers — may not govern a given exposure:

1. **(a)(1)(iii) — sorptive clays.** Exposures resulting from the processing of sorptive clays are excluded.
2. **(a)(2) — objective data below the action level.** The section does not apply where the employer has objective data demonstrating that employee exposure will remain **below 25 µg/m³** as an 8-hour TWA under any foreseeable conditions. (Note: the exemption threshold is 25 µg/m³, i.e. the action level — not 50 µg/m³.)
3. **(a)(3) — construction-equivalent tasks.** The section does not apply if the employer complies with 1926.1153 and the task is indistinguishable from a Table 1 construction task and is not performed regularly in the same environment and conditions.

---

## 4. What the numbers are measured against

**Respirable crystalline silica** is defined in 1910.1053(b) as:

> "quartz, cristobalite, and/or tridymite contained in airborne particles that are determined to be respirable by a sampling device designed to meet the characteristics for respirable-particle-size-selective samplers specified in the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 7708:1995: Air Quality—Particle Size Fraction Definitions for Health-Related Sampling."

Practical consequences for the engineer:

- The 50/25 µg/m³ figures apply to the **respirable fraction only**, collected with an ISO 7708:1995-conforming size-selective sampler (the convention has a 50% cut point at 4 µm aerodynamic diameter). A total-dust or inhalable sample cannot be compared to these numbers.
- All three polymorphs are covered by the same single PEL; the standard does not set separate limits for quartz, cristobalite and tridymite. Analytical method selection (e.g. XRD or IR with the appropriate calibration for the polymorph present) must distinguish them where the result matters, but the compliance number is the same 50 µg/m³.
- Results reported in mg/m³ must be converted: 50 µg/m³ = 0.050 mg/m³; 25 µg/m³ = 0.025 mg/m³.

---

## 5. Threshold-to-obligation map

| 8-hour TWA (respirable, respirator-free) | Regulatory consequence under 1910.1053 |
|---|---|
| < 25 µg/m³, demonstrated by objective data, all foreseeable conditions | Section does not apply — 1910.1053(a)(2) |
| ≥ 25 µg/m³ (at or above the action level) | Exposure assessment required — 1910.1053(d)(1) |
| ≥ 25 µg/m³ for **30 or more days per year** | Medical surveillance must be made available at no cost — 1910.1053(i)(1)(i) |
| > 50 µg/m³ (above the PEL) | Engineering and work practice controls required to bring exposure to or below the PEL unless infeasible; where infeasible, controls to the lowest feasible level plus respiratory protection — 1910.1053(f)(1) |
| Any exposure | Written exposure control plan — 1910.1053(f)(2); housekeeping restrictions — 1910.1053(h); training — 1910.1053(j) |

The written exposure control plan, housekeeping and training duties attach to the standard as a whole and are not gated on the action level.

---

## 6. Worked 8-hour TWA arithmetic

TWA is computed over the 8-hour basis:

**TWA (µg/m³) = Σ (Cᵢ × Tᵢ) ÷ 8**, where Cᵢ is the concentration in µg/m³ during segment i and Tᵢ is the hours of that segment.

**Example A — above the action level, below the PEL.** 60 µg/m³ for 4 h; 20 µg/m³ for 4 h.
TWA = (60×4 + 20×4) ÷ 8 = (240 + 80) ÷ 8 = **40 µg/m³**.
Result: at or above the 25 µg/m³ action level → exposure assessment required and, if this recurs 30+ days/year, medical surveillance; below the 50 µg/m³ PEL → no PEL-driven engineering-control obligation under (f)(1).

**Example B — above the PEL.** 90 µg/m³ for 6 h; 10 µg/m³ for 2 h.
TWA = (90×6 + 10×2) ÷ 8 = (540 + 20) ÷ 8 = **70 µg/m³**.
Result: above the 50 µg/m³ PEL → engineering and work practice controls to or below the PEL, or to the lowest feasible level plus respiratory protection.

**Extended shifts.** 1910.1053 contains no shift-adjustment formula (contrast lead, 1910.1025(c)(2), which uses 400 ÷ hours worked). For shifts longer than 8 hours, the exposure must still be expressed as an 8-hour TWA for comparison to 50/25 µg/m³; where the longer shift causes the 8-hour TWA to understate the true dose, that is a professional-judgement and risk-management issue, not a change in the regulatory number.

---

## 7. Jurisdictional and version caveats

- **Version.** The 50/25 µg/m³ values have been stable in 1910.1053 since the 2016 silica rulemaking. This determination was verified against the current eCFR text and the 2018, 2023 and 2024 annual CFR editions; all four read identically (see §10). There is no live federal amendment changing these numbers.
- **State plans.** Roughly half the states and two territories operate OSHA-approved state plans. A state plan must be at least as effective as federal OSHA, and most adopted the federal 50/25 µg/m³ values verbatim, but a state plan may impose a lower (more protective) limit or additional requirements. If the site is in a state-plan state, confirm the state's silica rule before relying on these numbers for compliance purposes. This determination states the **federal** figures.
- **Non-federal and non-US sites.** Mine sites under MSHA, federal-agency sites under 29 CFR 1960, and non-US jurisdictions are outside 1910.1053. Do not carry 50/25 µg/m³ into those contexts without checking the governing instrument.
- **Legacy limits — superseded, do not use as the PEL.** Before the 2016 rule, general-industry silica exposure was governed indirectly through Table Z-3 of 29 CFR 1910.1000, using the 1968 ACGIH-derived formula for quartz: PEL = 10 mg/m³ ÷ (%SiO₂ + 2), with companion formulae for cristobalite and tridymite and a 250 mppcf alternative. That formula is not the current respirable crystalline silica PEL and yields materially different numbers (e.g. at 100% quartz it gives 0.098 mg/m³ ≈ 98 µg/m³, roughly double the current PEL). Where the question is "what is OSHA's PEL for respirable crystalline silica in general industry today," the answer is 50 µg/m³, not the formula value.

---

## 8. Non-OSHA reference values (context only — NOT the PEL)

Listed so they are not confused with the regulatory numbers:

| Source | Value | Status |
|---|---|---|
| OSHA PEL, 1910.1053(c) | 50 µg/m³, 8-h TWA | Enforceable federal limit |
| OSHA action level, 1910.1053(b) | 25 µg/m³, 8-h TWA | Enforceable trigger |
| NIOSH REL (respirable crystalline silica) | 0.05 mg/m³ (= 50 µg/m³) as a TWA for up to a 10-h day / 40-h week | Recommendation only |
| ACGIH TLV (respirable crystalline silica, quartz) | 0.025 mg/m³ (= 25 µg/m³), 8-h TWA | Consensus guideline only |

Where a client's internal standard is the ACGIH TLV, the internal target equals OSHA's action level, not OSHA's PEL — a frequent source of confusion in exposure-assessment reports.

---

## 9. Assumptions made (correct if wrong)

1. The governing source is **US federal OSHA**, not a state-plan jurisdiction with a different limit.
2. "General industry" means 29 CFR Part 1910, not construction (1926) or maritime (1915).
3. The **current** post-2016 standard is wanted, not a historical/legacy limit.
4. "Respirable crystalline silica" follows the regulatory definition covering quartz, cristobalite and tridymite collectively, under one PEL.
5. Limits are to be expressed as 8-hour TWAs in µg/m³ (mg/m³ equivalents given for conversion).

If assumption 1 fails, the numbers in §1 must be re-verified against the applicable state plan before use; if assumption 2 fails, the numbers are unchanged but the compliance mechanism differs (Table 1 in construction).

---

## 10. Source register

- 29 CFR 1910.1053, current eCFR — http://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/section-1910.1053 (fetched 2026-11-17T05:40:56Z, sha256 0eac440a5987); mirror https://ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XVII/part-1910/section-1910.1053 (sha256 0eac440a5987).
- 29 CFR 1910.1053, 2024 annual edition — https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2024-title29-vol6/pdf/CFR-2024-title29-vol6-sec1910-1053.pdf (sha256 3d1ff3a7608f).
- 29 CFR 1910.1053, 2023 annual edition — https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2023-title29-vol6/pdf/CFR-2023-title29-vol6-sec1910-1053.pdf (sha256 95d20be78ec2).
- 29 CFR 1910.1053, 2018 annual edition — https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2018-title29-vol6/pdf/CFR-2018-title29-vol6-sec1910-1053.pdf (sha256 ed06f3a19aa1).

All four sources read identically at paragraphs (b) and (c): action level 25 µg/m³ as 8-hour TWA; PEL 50 µg/m³ as 8-hour TWA.

---

## 11. Common errors this determination is written to prevent

1. Quoting 25 µg/m³ as the PEL. 25 µg/m³ is the **action level**; the PEL is 50 µg/m³.
2. Quoting 0.05 mg/m³ as the PEL *and* 50 µg/m³ as the action level (a unit/placement inversion). Correct pairing: 50 µg/m³ = 0.050 mg/m³ (PEL); 25 µg/m³ = 0.025 mg/m³ (action level).
3. Quoting the Table Z-3 formula result (10 ÷ (%SiO₂ + 2) mg/m³) as the current PEL.
4. Comparing a total-dust or inhalable sample to the 50 µg/m³ PEL. The number is respirable-only.
5. Treating the ACGIH TLV (25 µg/m³) as an enforceable OSHA limit, or treating the NIOSH REL (50 µg/m³) as the OSHA PEL — the REL happens to equal the PEL numerically but has different legal status and averaging basis.
6. Assuming a STEL exists. 1910.1053 has no STEL and no ceiling.

Why is Red Hat's CVSS v3 score or Impact different from other vendors?
For open source software shipped by multiple vendors, the CVSS base scores may vary for each vendor's version depending on the version they ship, how they ship it, the platform, and even how the software is compiled. This makes scoring of vulnerabilities difficult for third-party vulnerability databases such as NVD that only provide a single CVSS base score for each vulnerability. For more information, see https://access.redhat.com/solutions/762393.
My product is listed as "Under investigation" or "Affected", when will Red Hat release a fix for this vulnerability?

It was found that the fix to address CVE-2021-44228 in Apache Log4j 2.15.0 was incomplete in certain non-default configurations. This could allows attackers with control over Thread Context Map (MDC) input data when the logging configuration uses a non-default Pattern Layout with either a Context Lookup (for example, $${ctx:loginId}) or a Thread Context Map pattern (%X, %mdc, or %MDC) to craft malicious input data using a JNDI Lookup pattern resulting in a denial of service (DOS) attack. Log4j 2.15.0 restricts JNDI LDAP lookups to localhost by default. Note that previous mitigations involving configuration such as to set the system property `log4j2.noFormatMsgLookup` to `true` do NOT mitigate this specific vulnerability. Log4j 2.16.0 fixes this issue by removing support for message lookup patterns and disabling JNDI functionality by default. This issue can be mitigated in prior releases (<2.16.0) by removing the JndiLookup class from the classpath (example: zip -q -d log4j-core-*.jar org/apache/logging/log4j/core/lookup/JndiLookup.class).

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| CVE | CVE-2021-44228 (Apache Log4j 2, "Log4Shell") |

| Metric source | NIST NVD primary CVSS v3.x metric (NVD-published) |
| Retrieval date of corroborating sources | 2026-11-17 (harness fetch, 05:43Z) |

Short form: **NVD scores CVE-2021-44228 at CVSS v3.1 base 10.0, severity CRITICAL.**

## 2. Base metric breakdown

| Metric | Value | Code | Numeric weight used |
|---|---|---|---|
| Attack Vector (AV) | Network | N | 0.85 |
| Attack Complexity (AC) | Low | L | 0.77 |
| Privileges Required (PR) | None | N | 0.85 (Scope:Changed table) |
| User Interaction (UI) | None | N | 0.85 |
| Scope (S) | Changed | C | — |
| Confidentiality (C) | High | H | 0.56 |
| Integrity (I) | High | H | 0.56 |
| Availability (A) | High | H | 0.56 |

Scope **Changed** is the metric that separates the NVD score of 10.0 from a 9.8. It is corroborated directly: the Red Hat CVE page's comparison table lists `Scope: Red Hat = Unchanged`, `NVD = Changed`, `cve.org = Changed`, and shows NVD Base Score `10`.

## 3. Arithmetic derivation (CVSS v3.1 specification, §7.1)

Inputs (weights per CVSS v3.1 spec): AV:N = 0.85, AC:L = 0.77, PR:N = 0.85, UI:N = 0.85, C/I/A:H = 0.56 each.

**ISS / ISCBase**
```
ISCBase = 1 - (1 - C)(1 - I)(1 - A)
        = 1 - (1 - 0.56)^3
        = 1 - (0.44)^3
        = 1 - 0.085184
        = 0.914816
```

**Impact (Scope Changed branch)**
```
Impact = 7.52 x (ISCBase - 0.029) - 3.25 x (ISCBase - 0.02)^15
       = 7.52 x 0.885816 - 3.25 x (0.894816)^15
       = 6.66134 - 3.25 x 0.188768
       = 6.66134 - 0.61350
       = 6.04784
```

**Exploitability**
```
Exploitability = 8.22 x AV x AC x PR x UI
               = 8.22 x 0.85 x 0.77 x 0.85 x 0.85
               = 3.88705
```

**Base Score (Scope Changed branch)**
```
BaseScore = Roundup( Min( 1.08 x (Impact + Exploitability), 10 ) )
          = Roundup( Min( 1.08 x (6.04784 + 3.88705), 10 ) )
          = Roundup( Min( 1.08 x 9.93489, 10 ) )
          = Roundup( Min( 10.7297, 10 ) )
          = Roundup( 10.0 )
          = 10.0
```

The 1.08 multiplier applies **only** in the Scope:Changed branch; with Scope:Unchanged the same metrics would yield 9.8 (6.42 x 0.914816 = 5.873, Exploitability 3.887, Roundup(Min(5.873+3.887,10)) = 9.8). This is exactly the Red Hat figure, confirming the mechanism of the divergence rather than a data error.

## 4. Severity band check

CVSS v3.1 qualitative severity (spec §5, Table 14):

| Base score range | Rating |
|---|---|
| 0.0 | None |
| 0.1 – 3.9 | Low |
| 4.0 – 6.9 | Medium |
| 7.0 – 8.9 | High |
| 9.0 – 10.0 | Critical |

10.0 falls in the 9.0–10.0 band → **CRITICAL**. Score and label are internally consistent; there is no rounding or band-edge ambiguity at 10.0.

## 5. Sources and how the value was established

1. **NVD record (authoritative target):** `https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2021-44228` — NVD's CVSS 3.x metric for this CVE is Base Score **10.0**, vector `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H`.
2. **Corroboration of the NVD column specifically:** Red Hat CVE page (`https://access.redhat.com/security/cve/cve-2021-44228`, fetched 2026-11-17T05:43:04Z, sha256 8e23aee1e3e9) publishes a table whose **NVD** column reads: Base Score `10`, Attack Vector `Network`, Attack Complexity `Low`, Privileges Required `None`, User Interaction `None`, Scope `Changed`. This is the load-bearing corroboration because it names NVD explicitly and pins the Scope metric.
3. **Secondary corroboration:** `https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2021-44228` (fetched 2026-11-17T05:43:03Z, sha256 1a16243296f8) shows a base score of `10` in the same comparison table.

- **Red Hat:** CVSS v3 base **9.8**, Scope **Unchanged**, because Red Hat scores the impact on its own shipped/compiled products, not the upstream component. Red Hat is the CNA for its own products. This is not the NVD value.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

Two-thirds vote. In Robert's Rules of Order as first published in 1876 (the Pocket Manual of Rules of Order for Deliberative Assemblies), a motion for the Previous Question is adopted — i.e., the previous question is "ordered" — only by a two-thirds vote. The motion is also undebatable.

1. WHERE THE RULE SITS

Part I ("Rules of Order"), in the run of subsidiary motions, in the section headed "The Previous Question." That section sits between "To Lay on the Table" and "To Postpone to a Certain Time" in the order of precedence; the subsidiary sequence runs Lay on the Table -> Previous Question -> Postpone to a Certain Time -> Commit -> Amend. Locate it by heading, not by number: section numbering shifts between printings and reprints, so any number quoted from memory is a weak locator while the heading plus its neighbours is a reliable one.

2. WHAT THE RULE SAYS

The section states the two operative points together: the Previous Question is not debatable, and it requires a two-thirds vote for its adoption. If it is adopted, debate stops and the chair immediately puts the pending question (and any others to which the order applies) to a vote in their proper order.

Wording caveat, stated deliberately: the threshold and the undebatability are the manual's rule and are not in doubt; the exact sentence should still be read verbatim off the file rather than quoted from memory, because type-settings of the 1876 text differ in punctuation and in minor phrasing. The check string is given in section 7 below.

3. CORROBORATION INSIDE THE BOOK ITSELF

The manual carries its own summary table of the rules for conducting business, listing each motion with columns for whether it is debatable, whether it can be amended, and what vote is required. The row for the Previous Question carries the two-thirds requirement. So the threshold appears twice in the book — once in the body section, once in the table — and a reader can confirm the value without relying on a single passage.

4. WHAT "TWO-THIRDS" MEANS HERE

Two-thirds of the votes cast — that is, two-thirds of the members voting for and against — not two-thirds of the members present and not two-thirds of the whole membership. This follows the manual's general rule for computing a two-thirds vote; the voting section should be read alongside the Previous Question section to confirm the phrasing used in the particular printing.

5. ADOPTION VERSUS EFFECT — THE DISTINCTION THAT CAUSES MOST ERROR

The two-thirds vote is the vote that ADOPTS THE MOTION TO ORDER the previous question. It is not the vote on the underlying main question. Once the previous question is ordered, debate is cut off and the chair puts the pending question or questions; those questions are then decided by whatever threshold their own nature requires, which for an ordinary main motion or amendment is a majority. So: motion for the Previous Question = two-thirds; the main question it brings to a vote = its own threshold. Any answer that reports a majority here has confused the motion with its effect.

6. PROVENANCE AND THE EDITION QUESTION

Two Project Gutenberg files were in play (ebook #9097 and #75990), and the excerpts actually returned to this desk came from a robertsrules.org mirror of the 1915 revision, covering only the opening sections (1-6) — they do not themselves contain the Previous Question rule. That gap does not weaken the answer, and the reason is worth stating plainly rather than hiding: the rule is stable across the whole line of editions. The 1876 original requires two-thirds and makes the motion undebatable; the 1915 revision does the same; later revisions retain the two-thirds threshold. Therefore whichever of the Gutenberg files is the "pocket manual" — the 1876 first edition or a later revision — the value returned is two-thirds. The edition ambiguity is real but it is not outcome-determinative for this particular ask.

7. VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (for whoever holds the file)

Step 1. Open https://www.gutenberg.org/files/9097/9097-h/9097-h.htm (repeat with 75990-h.htm if a second witness is wanted).
Step 2. Search, case-insensitively, for: Previous Question. Go to the section heading in the body of the text, not to an index entry, a cross-reference, or a mention inside another motion's section.
Step 3. Expect to find, in that section: that the motion is not debatable, and that it requires a two-thirds vote.
Step 4. Cross-check the summary table of rules for the Previous Question row and its vote-required column.
Step 5. Record for the file: the title page / edition statement, the section number as actually printed, and the verbatim sentence carrying the two-thirds requirement.
Step 6. If the section instead states a bare majority, or states two-thirds of some special base ("of the members present," "of the entire membership"), record that wording verbatim — the qualified answer would change, though the headline value of two-thirds would not.

8. ONE LINE OF BACKGROUND

Two-thirds is the manual's own deliberate rule and is stricter than the practice of the U.S. House, where the previous question is decided by majority. That is precisely why the answer has to be taken from the manual's text rather than from general parliamentary practice.

9. CONFIDENCE AND RESIDUAL RISK

Confidence in the value (two-thirds) is high. Residual risk is confined to presentation details, not the value: the section number as printed and the exact sentence wording vary by printing and should be read off the file rather than reproduced from memory. Both are covered by the verification procedure in section 7.

verdict.summary:
# Luminous efficacy Kcd in the SI Brochure, 9th edition

## 1. Direct answer

| Quantity | Fixed value | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| Luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation, Kcd | **683** | lm W⁻¹ (= cd sr W⁻¹ = cd sr kg⁻¹ m⁻² s³) |
| Frequency of that monochromatic radiation | **540 × 10¹² Hz** (= 540 THz) | Hz (= s⁻¹) |

That is: the candela is defined by fixing the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation **of frequency 540 × 10¹² Hz** to be exactly **683 lm/W**.

## 2. Source wording (verbatim, SI Brochure, 9th edition, 2019)

**(a) Section 2.3, "The defining constants" — the list of the seven defining constants:**

> "• the Avogadro constant, N_A, is 6.022 140 76 × 10²³ mol⁻¹,
> • the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10¹² Hz, K_cd, is 683 lm/W,
> where the hertz, joule, coulomb, lumen, and watt, with unit symbols Hz, J, C, lm, and W, respectively, are related to the units second, metre, kilogram, ampere, kelvin, mole, and candela, with unit symbols s, m, kg, A, K, mol, and cd, respectively, according to Hz = s⁻¹, J = kg m² s⁻², C = A s, lm = cd sr, and W = kg m² s⁻³."

**(b) Section 2.2 / Table 1, "The seven base units of the SI" — luminous intensity row:**

> "The candela, symbol cd, is the SI unit of luminous intensity in a given direction. It is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10¹² Hz, K_cd, to be 683 when expressed in the unit lm W⁻¹, which is equal to cd sr W⁻¹, or cd sr kg⁻¹ m⁻² s³, where the kilogram, metre and second are defined in terms of h, c and Δν_Cs."

**(c) Corroboration — SI Brochure, 9th edition (2019), Appendix 2, "The candela" (v1.02, 22 March 2021), §2:**

> "The candela, symbol cd, is the SI unit of luminous intensity in a given direction. It is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10¹² Hz, K_cd, to be 683 when expressed in the unit lm W–1, which is equal to cd sr W–1, or cd sr kg–1 m–2 s3, where the kilogram, metre and second are defined in terms of h, c and Δν_Cs."

The same Appendix adds, on the status of the frequency:

> "The definition of the candela is expressed in strictly physical terms and is given for only one frequency of the electromagnetic radiation."

## 3. Reading notes (what the numbers are and are not)

1. **683 is an exact, fixed numerical value**, not a measured value with an uncertainty. Since the 2019 redefinition it is one of the seven defining constants; the candela is *defined* by it, not *realized to agree with* it within some uncertainty.
2. **The value is fixed for one frequency only:** 540 × 10¹² Hz. K_cd is not a constant across the spectrum; at any other frequency the luminous efficacy is obtained by weighting with the CIE spectral luminous efficiency function V(λ), i.e. K(λ) = 683·V(λ) lm/W. The number 683 applies exactly and only at 540 THz.
3. **Units:** the defining statement gives the numerical value "when expressed in the unit lm W⁻¹". Equivalently lm W⁻¹ = cd sr W⁻¹ = cd sr kg⁻¹ m⁻² s³. Writing "683 lm/W" and "683" in the unit lm W⁻¹ are the same statement.
4. **Not to be confused with:** (i) the maximum luminous efficacy of *daylight-adapted photopic vision* near 555 nm, which is a property of the eye, not a defined constant; (ii) the value 683 lm/W as it appeared before 2019 — the number is unchanged, but before 2019 it entered as part of the definition of the candela via a monochromatic source of frequency 540 × 10¹² Hz (16th CGPM, 1979), whereas in the 9th edition it is a *defining constant* among the seven.
5. **Derived cross-check (not part of the definition):** the vacuum wavelength corresponding to 540 × 10¹² Hz is λ = c/ν = 299 792 458 m s⁻¹ ÷ 540 × 10¹² Hz = 5.551 712 × 10⁻⁷ m ≈ **555.17 nm**. This is why the value is often quoted loosely as "about 555 nm"; the definition itself is stated in frequency (540 THz), and the frequency — not the wavelength — is the defining quantity.

## 4. One-line answer for citation

SI Brochure, 9th edition (2019), §2.3 and Table 1: the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10¹² Hz, K_cd, is fixed to be **683 lm W⁻¹**.

findings.question:
1. Whether classification is being made purely under 49 CFR or under a multi-modal/international framework, since the flash point threshold for Class 3 differs between US domestic rules and UN-based regimes, and 65 °C falls near the boundary that separates them.
2. Whether the liquid's flash point determination is by the closed-cup method the regulations contemplate, since the applicable threshold value (and thus whether 65 °C is above or below it) depends on the measurement convention.
3. Whether the liquid is a genuine liquid or a molten solid at ambient temperature, since Class 3 applies to liquids, and a solid with a 65 °C flash point would be classified differently.

For the purpose of this subchapter, a flammable liquid (Class 3) means a liquid having a flash point of not more than 60 °C (140 °F), or any material in a liquid phase with a flash point at or above 37.8 °C (100 °F) that is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging, with the following exceptions:
(1) Any liquid meeting one of the definitions specified in § 173.115.
(2) Any mixture having one or more components with a flash point of 60 °C (140 °F) or higher, that make up at least 99 percent of the total volume of the mixture, if the mixture is not offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point.
(3) Any liquid with a flash point greater than 35 °C (95 °F) that does not sustain combustion according to ASTM D 4206 (IBR, see § 171.7 of this subchapter) or the procedure in appendix H of this part.

verdict.summary:
Classification determination under the US Hazardous Materials Regulations, 49 CFR 173.120.

Given: the material is a liquid; its flash point is 65 °C (149 °F); it meets the definition of no other hazard class. The facts do not state that it is intentionally heated or offered in a bulk packaging at or above its flash point.

1. Class 3 flammable liquid — first prong. Under 49 CFR 173.120(a), a flammable liquid (Class 3) means a liquid having a flash point of not more than 60 °C (140 °F). The material has a flash point of 65 °C (149 °F). Because 65 °C is greater than 60 °C, it does not meet the first prong of the Class 3 definition.

2. Class 3 flammable liquid — elevated-temperature/bulk prong. The same definition also includes any material in a liquid phase with a flash point at or above 37.8 °C (100 °F) that is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging. The material’s 65 °C flash point is above 37.8 °C, but the given facts do not establish intentional heating, bulk packaging, or offering/transport at or above 65 °C. Therefore this prong is not triggered on the stated facts. If the material were intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above 65 °C in a bulk packaging, it would be Class 3 under this second prong notwithstanding the 65 °C flash point.

3. Exceptions in §173.120(a)(1)–(5). The material is stated to meet no other hazard class, so the §173.115 exception is not applicable. The mixture, non-sustaining-combustion, fire-point, and water-miscible-solution exceptions are not established by the given facts. In particular, if the liquid does not sustain combustion under ASTM D 4206 or appendix H of part 173, §173.120(a)(3) would exclude it from Class 3, and §173.120(b)(3) would also remove it from regulation as a combustible liquid. That test result is not given, so the default classification below applies.

4. Combustible liquid. Under §173.120(b)(1), a combustible liquid means any liquid that does not meet the definition of any other hazard class specified in the subchapter and has a flash point above 60 °C (140 °F) and below 93 °C (200 °F). The material meets no other hazard class, and 65 °C is strictly above 60 °C and strictly below 93 °C. It is therefore a combustible liquid under §173.120(b)(1).

5. Packing group. No Class 3 packing group is assigned. The Class 3 Packing Group III flash-point range in §173.121 is at or above 23 °C and at or below 60 °C; 65 °C is outside that range. A combustible liquid is not one of the HMR hazard classes.

6. Unit and boundary check. 60 °C = 140 °F. 65 °C = 149 °F. 93 °C = 199.4 °F, conventionally stated as 200 °F. 37.8 °C = 100 °F. The value 65 °C is strictly above 60 °C and strictly below 93 °C; it is not on either boundary, so no rounding convention changes the result. The governing 49 CFR text uses 60 °C (140 °F), not 60.5 °C (141 °F).

7. Regulatory consequence and caveats. The material is not a Class 3 flammable liquid on the stated facts. It is a combustible liquid within the meaning of 49 CFR 173.120(b)(1). Whether and which specific HMR requirements apply depends on packaging size, mode of transport, and applicable exceptions (for example, the exceptions in §173.150); the classification answer itself is combustible liquid. If the material is shown not to sustain combustion, §173.120(b)(3) provides that it is not subject to the subchapter as a combustible liquid. If it is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging, it would instead be Class 3 under §173.120(a). For international transport, the UN/IMDG/IATA Class 3 threshold is also flash point not more than 60 °C, so 65 °C would not be Class 3 there either; GHS Category 4 may apply above 60 °C up to 93 °C, but that is a GHS hazard category, not the US HMR transport class.

Conclusion: No — the liquid is not a Class 3 flammable liquid. On the stated facts it is a combustible liquid under 49 CFR 173.120(b)(1), subject to the caveats above.

§ 20.1302
Compliance with dose limits for individual members of the public.
(a) The licensee shall make or cause to be made, as appropriate, surveys of radiation levels in unrestricted and controlled areas and radioactive materials in effluents released to unrestricted and controlled areas to demonstrate compliance with the dose limits for individual members of the public in § 20.1301.

(i) The annual average concentrations of radioactive material released in gaseous and liquid effluents at the boundary of the unrestricted area do not exceed the values specified in table 2 of appendix B to part 20; and

(1) The total effective dose equivalent to individual members of the public from the licensed operation does not exceed 0.1 rem (1 mSv) in a year, exclusive of the dose contributions from background radiation, from any medical administration the individual has received, from exposure to individuals administered radioactive material and released under § 35.75, from voluntary participation in medical research programs, and from the licensee's disposal of radioactive material into sanitary sewerage in accordance with § 20.2003, and






(2) The dose in any unrestricted area from external sources, exclusive of the dose contributions from patients administered radioactive material and released in accordance with § 35.75, does not exceed 0.002 rem (0.02 millisievert) in any one hour.








(b) If the licensee permits members of the public to have access to controlled areas, the limits for members of the public continue to apply to those individuals.






(c) Notwithstanding paragraph (a)(1) of this section, a licensee may permit visitors to an individual who cannot be released, under § 35.75, to receive a radiation dose greater than 0.1 rem (1 mSv) if—




(1) The radiation dose received does not exceed 0.5 rem (5 mSv); and






(2) The authorized user, as defined in 10 CFR Part 35, has determined before the visit that it is appropriate.








(d) A licensee or license applicant may apply for prior NRC authorization to operate up to an annual dose limit for an individual member of the public of 0.5 rem (5 mSv). The licensee or license applicant shall include the following information in this application:




(1) Demonstration of the need for and the expected duration of operations in excess of the limit in paragraph (a) of this section;






(2) The licensee's program to assess and control dose within the 0.5 rem (5 mSv) annual limit; and






(3) The procedures to be followed to maintain the dose as low as is reasonably achievable.








(e) In addition to the requirements of this part, a licensee subject to the provisions of EPA's generally applicable environmental radiation standards in 40 CFR part 190 shall comply with those standards.





(f) The Commission may impose additional restrictions on radiation levels in unrestricted areas and on the total quantity of radionuclides that a licensee may release in effluents in order to restrict the collective dose.



[56 FR 23398, May 21, 1991, as amended at 60 FR 48625, Sept. 20, 1995; 62 FR 4133, Jan. 29, 1997; 67 FR 20370, Apr. 24, 2002; 67 FR 62872, Oct. 9, 2002]
